Homage to Śrī Heruka.
The supreme essence of all phenomena, which removes fear from all phenomena;
it is the non-appearance of all phenomena, yet the illuminator of all phenomena. //1//
Having prostrated to that Great Hero, who is equal to space and as stainless as space, I shall write this commentary (*pañjikā*) on the *Cakrasaṃvara-tantra*. (2)

Regarding this, having restated the objection—namely, why the compiler did not provide an introduction (upodghāta) at the very beginning of the tantra with the words "Thus have I [heard]" and so forth—some explain it as a means of resolution, saying that it was for the sake of demonstrating the Blessed One’s non-abiding nirvāṇa.
He clarifies this very point by stating: "He always abides within the self of all."

Others, however, maintain that because [this tantra] was extracted from the *Khasama*, the root-tantra of one hundred thousand [verses], and because it was already indicated at the very beginning of that root-tantra with the words "Thus [it was said]" (*evam*) and so forth, it was not repeated here in this subsequent tantra (*uttaratantra*).
Therefore, he says: "The 'subsequent' (*uttara*) is the external statement of meanings that were absorbed into other tantras."
Others, however, maintain that the identity of the teacher and the taught is indicated by the fact that the nature of reality (*dharmatā*) cannot be disclosed;
for it is said that "the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, are the very embodiment of the *tantra*.

First of all, even those who follow the Dharma (*dharmānusārin*), being discerning individuals, engage with this work only after having thoroughly examined the relationship between the expression and the expressed, as well as the purpose and the ultimate purpose thereof.
For this very reason, they are so designated.
Now, beginning with "atha ata" and ending with "iti śrīherukābhidhāne," this entire textual composition is the *Abhidhāna-cakrasaṃvara*.
Therefore, that which is to be expressed—the form of the tantras such as Śrī Heruka and Vajravārāhī—is the subject matter (abhidheya).

Some say that the relationship is characterized by the signifier and the signified; others say that the relationship is characterized by the nature of the means and the goal. The purpose [of this work] extends from the Blessed One’s entry into the mandala for the sake of those to be trained, up to the secret empowerment.
The attainment of that fruit at a subsequent time is the "purpose of the purpose" (*prayojana-prayojana*).
[1.2] By means of the collection of particles beginning with *atha*, he determines that this work follows upon the preceding treatise (*uttara-tantra*).
*Atha* signifies immediate succession; the connection is: immediately after the *Khasama-tantra*, I shall speak—that is, I will declare—this which is about to be stated. [1.3]
Regarding the word *ataḥ* ("therefore"), since it signifies both sequence and cause, and since it would have been perfectly clear to say "immediately after that" (*tadanantaram*),
the employment of the word *atha* is for the purpose of auspiciousness (*maṅgala*).

The opening words of a treatise, such as *maṅgala* and so forth, are for the sake of removing obstacles for the listeners, or for the purpose of indicating the subject matter (*adhikāra*). For this very reason it has been said: "They say that the word *atha* refers either to an auspicious beginning (*maṅgala*) with reference to what was previously discussed, or to the subject matter (*adhikārika*); whereas the word *ataḥ* is used in a treatise to indicate the sense of sequence and cause."

What is that which is about to be explained? He says: it is the secret (*rahasya*), because it is to be concealed from all the śrāvakas and others, as it is not to be revealed to them. Alternatively, it is the secret because it is that which is to be accomplished through the unification of wisdom (*prajñā*) and skillful means (*upāya*). Alternatively, the three—vajra, lotus, and bodhicitta—are the secret.
The letter *ra* is declared to be the vajra, and the letter *ha* is called the lotus; the seed-syllable of both of these is also designated as *syam*. (3)
Because the letter *ra* has the form of a vajra-needle,
because the letter *ha* has the form of a bird’s beak,
and because the conjunction of the letters *sa* and *ya* has the nature of both seeds.
And because of the inclusion of this [root] *syandū*, which has lost its final consonant, as "śravaṇa" (hearing), according to the ultimate truth.
Manifesting the thought, "How shall I speak? he says "in brief" (samāsāt), meaning "from the summary," with the intention that [it was] "excessively extensive in the *Khasama-tantra*.
Manifesting that very same point, he says, "but not in detail" (*na tu vistarāt*).
Alternatively, the connection is: "not, however, in brief; rather, in detail."

The intended meaning here is as follows: while in the *Khasama-tantra* there is an extensive treatment of both the subject matter and the text, in this [work], however, there is an extensive treatment of the subject matter alone, because the three wheels consisting of the triple world are to be explained. [1.4]
Now, he specifies the secret itself with four words.
The word *śrī* denotes worship.
In this tantra, *Heruka* is the designation for the Lord, the sovereign. Śrī-Heruka is Heruka who is preeminent in auspiciousness (*śrī*).
His union with the Blessed Lady Vajravārāhī is an embrace in the state of equal flavor (samarasa).
Because the Blessed One Heruka consists of the three realms, his designation by means of these three syllables is indeed appropriate.
Alternatively, it is because he consists of the threefold non-apprehension: all phenomena are devoid of cause, all phenomena are devoid of conceptualization, and all phenomena do not abide anywhere.
Alternatively, "Śrī Heruka" is the noun to be qualified (*viśeṣya*) and "secret" (*rahasya*) is the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*).
For this very reason, it is appropriate that "the accomplisher of all desires and aims" is a qualifier of the Blessed One;
for "all desires" refers to all wishes.
That very thing is the goal, which is the purpose; the Blessed One is its accomplisher;
therefore, [the word "to him" refers to] him.
Alternatively, it is a descriptive compound (viśeṣaṇasamāsa) consisting of "all" and "those desires."

It is said that it is "even higher than the higher" because there is no distinction between the taught and the teacher; thus, it is superior even to those *uttaratantras* such as the *Samāja* and others.

Regarding the term *ḍākinījālāsaṃvaram*: all the *ḍākinīs* are established within the three wheels (*tricakra*); their "net" (*jāla*) is their assembly. "Saṃvara" means their concealment, that is, their protection or hiding.
The ḍākinīs are those who travel through the sky; from the root *ḍai*, meaning "to go through the air," the sense is that they fly or soar upward.

Alternatively, because it acts like a net (*jāla*)—insofar as it restrains the outward movement of the *ḍākinīs* who are by nature prone to flying up—it is called the "Binding of the Net of Ḍākinīs" (*ḍākinījālasaṃvara*).
Therefore, the connection is with the word "therein" (*tatra*).
Now, demonstrating the majesty of the Blessed Lord Śrī Heruka through his sovereignty, he first shows the excellence of the location.
Regarding the term "secret" (*rahasya*): here, by the word "secret," all *ḍākinīs* residing within the three wheels (*tricakra*) are designated.
In that secret place, the "secret practice" (*rahasya*) consists of the convergence of the entire realm of space (*ākāśadhātu*) into a single form through the state of equal flavor (*samarasatā*).
It is the abode of the Blessed One Śrī Heruka, joined with Vajravārāhī and the others.
To the question "Of what specific nature is that?", he says: "Supreme" (*paramam*).
It is supreme, excellent, preeminent, and unsurpassed, because it is the foundation for both mundane and supramundane knowledge.
Furthermore, what is its specific quality? It is "delightful" (*ramya*).
It is delightful because it is charming due to the activity of the play of unsurpassed worship.

[1.6] Now, he states the non-differentiation of the perfection of the assembly by saying, "always abiding in the self of all. The "self" (*ātman*) of all those established within the three wheels of the nature of the triple world is their own body or essential form. By saying "always" (*sadā*), he indicates the absence of separation at any place or at any time. By saying "abiding" (*sthita*), he implies that, by transcending the triple world, it possesses a single mode of being and an indestructible nature. [1.7]
Now he distinguishes the perfection of sovereignty.
Regarding the phrase "consisting of all ḍākinīs," the word *ḍākinī* is merely illustrative; it should be understood as "consisting of all ḍākas and ḍākinīs.
The suffix *-mayaṭ* is used here in the sense of essence (*svabhāva*) or cause (*hetu*), meaning that they have become one in a single, unified state (*ekalolībhūta*).
He is a *sattva* because of his capacity to accomplish the welfare of all beings; or he is a *sattva* because of his possession of the quality of supreme sovereignty.
He is called Vajra because he is indivisible.
He is Vajrasattva because, through vajra-wisdom, he has ascended to the welfare of all sentient beings;
or alternatively, he is Vajrasattva because his being (*sattva*) cannot be shaken by anyone at all, such as Hari, Hara, and others.
Or, because its intrinsic nature consists of wisdom and skillful means,
it is said to be supreme and most excellent by virtue of its utility for the accomplishment of the welfare of oneself and others.
Because his nature consists of unsurpassed worship, supreme passion, bliss, and mental well-being, the Blessed One himself is bliss;
the word "bliss" (sukha) is always neuter in gender.
By these [verses], the perfection of one's own and others' welfare has been stated.
In response to the doubt as to whether this is merely another qualification of the deity, he says "for he," etc., in order to dispel that doubt.
The word "hi" is used in the sense of restriction.
He is called "Self-Existent" (svayaṃbhū) because he exists by himself;
the meaning is that he is not produced by another.
And so it has been said:
"That mind which, because of its firmness, is called 'sattva' by all beings..."
Through meditative absorption, absorption indeed attains the state of a vajra by means of certainties;
furthermore, through the yoga of the empowerment of sentient beings, one becomes Vajrasattva.
(4) % STTS 2531–2532ab with *vajrasamaḥ* for *samādhis tu*
And since he is not created by anyone, he is called "Self-Existent" (svayambhū).
He is the Blessed One (Bhagavān) because of his endowment with good fortune;
he is the Blessed One because of his crushing of the four enemies that are the Māras;
he is the Blessed One because of his crushing of the afflictions such as passion.
He is called the Blessed One (Bhagavān) because he is endowed with the six qualities beginning with sovereignty (aiśvarya).
And so it has been said:
"The traditional teaching holds that 'Bhaga' refers to the sixfold [perfections]: complete sovereignty, beauty, fame, splendor, knowledge, and effort toward one's goals. (5)
This has already been cited by Vilāsavajra and Haribhadra:
"For he is the hero"—this should be connected as "he alone is the hero.
This is for the purpose of excluding the possibility of another [possessing] heroism, just as in the expression "Pārtha is the archer."
Alternatively, non-duality is stated because he consists of the essence of the twenty-four heroes. For this very reason, the Blessed One is the *Ḍākinījālasaṃvara*.

Now, in order to indicate the stage of accomplishment (*niṣpattikrama*) of that Blessed One who belongs to the three wheels, he says, beginning with "From the source, from the sound... and ending with "...listen to what is proclaimed in the tantra."
And that is being stated briefly according to the instruction of the Guru.

This is its sequence: first, having sat down in a place favorable to the mind, having placed a pill made of the five nectars in the mouth, the mantra-practitioner, facing the southern direction, having conjured up the ground of a most terrifying great cremation ground, and having uttered three times, "May I become Śrī Heruka for the sake of the welfare and happiness of all sentient beings," he should instantly manifest the form of the Great Seal (mahāmudrā) as described below, joined with his own deity, arising from the syllable *HŪṂ*. Then, having uttered the vowels and consonants (*ālikāli*) three times, [he says] "Heruka."

Having placed the three syllables in sequence upon the head, throat, and heart, one should personally cause oneself and all external stable and moving objects to become non-manifest, [realizing] that "all phenomena are free from causes, all phenomena are free from conceptualization, and all phenomena do not abide anywhere. Then, by the power of previous vows, one perceives the three syllables *oṃ āḥ hūṃ* in the space above, below, and in between respectively; from the transformation of the syllable *hūṃ*, there arises a vajra, and within the hub (*varaṭaka*) of that vajra is the syllable *hūṃ*.

The rays of light in the form of syllables that issued forth from those [syllables], pervading the hollow of space as far as the Cakravāḍa mountains, performed the welfare of all sentient beings; then, having returned there by means of rays shaped like elephant goads (*parivṛttāṅkuśa*), they entered back into those three syllables: the *oṃ* into the *āḥ*, the *āḥ* into the *huṃ* within the vajra in due order, the vajra-needle and so forth into the hub (*varaṭaka*) of the vajra, the hub of the vajra also into the *huṃ*, the *ū* into the *ha*, the *ha* into the head (*śiras*), and the head into the half-moon shape, and that too—

Having caused the drop (*bindu*) to enter the resonance (*nāda*), and the resonance to enter the mere resonance (*nādamātra*), and having established that mere resonance free from all objective perception, one should, for the sake of purifying the receptacle world (*bhājanaloka*), generate the mandalas of wind, fire, earth, gold, and water. Upon these, by means of the syllable *ka*, one generates a tortoise or a skull-cup; upon that, by means of the syllable *aḥ*, a double vajra (*viśvavajra*); upon that, by means of the syllable *paṃ*, an eight-petaled lotus; and upon that, by means of the syllable *suṃ*, Mount Sumeru, square and composed of the four jewels.

Above that, having meditated upon a lotus, and upon it a moon mandala surrounded by bees resting on the filaments of the lotus, one should visualize from the mere sound situated in the space of the sky the syllable *HŪṂ* appearing in sequence upon the moon mandala. From its transformation, one visualizes the Blessed One joined with Vajravārāhī, possessing twelve arms; with his first two hands holding a vajra and a vajra-bell, he embraces the Goddess, while his second two hands hold an elephant hide dripping with blood behind his back.

He holds a trident, an axe, a vetālī, and a *ḍamaru* with his four right hands, and a vajra, a *khaṭvāṅga*, a skull-cup, and the head of Brahmā with his four left hands; he is endowed with the six *mudrās*, adorned with a crown of matted hair marked at the top by a double-vajra (*viśvavajra*), with a crescent moon as a crest on the left side, beautified below by five skulls, wearing a garland of vajras, and possessing three eyes. His primary face and entire body have the luster of a fresh rain-cloud, while the left face is dark blue and the rear face is red.

The left face is yellow; he has a sacrificial thread (*yajñopavīta*) consisting of a garland of human heads encircled by the vowels and consonants; he is clothed in a fresh tiger skin; he stands in the *ālīḍha* posture, treading upon the Lord of Beings (*bhūtapati*); he is mounted upon the filaments of a lotus; he is surrounded by four goddesses; and he resides within the interior of a triple wheel—these and other details will be elaborated upon later.

Vajravārāhī is free of ashes, endowed with the five mudrās, adorned with a girdle of bones and so forth, naked, with disheveled hair, her right hand raised holding a vajra, embracing [the consort] at the neck, her left hand holding a skull-cup with two openings filled with human blood and intestines, and standing in the *pratyālīḍha* posture; these and other details we shall explain in the northern section [1.11].
Regarding the term "from arising" (*saṃbhavāt*), it is indicated by a word in the form of a sound (a noun) in the ablative case used as a coordinate [genitive];
the meaning is "from the arising of the union of the two organs."
Therefore, from the sound situated in the space of the sky— *hi* meaning "because"—
the plural form "they have emerged" is used in order to indicate that all the heroes (*vīra*) and *ḍākinīs*, who possess the three wheels, have emerged from a single sound.
Of what nature are they? They are "those whose sphere of activity is the conduct of the *samaya*.

*Samaya* is twofold: that which is to be protected and that which is to be consumed. Their "conduct" (*ācāra*) is their practice or engagement; those for whom this very [conduct] is the sphere or domain are so described.
Alternatively, *samayas* are the goddesses; their conduct is the subject matter, and the heroes are those whose sphere of activity is that [conduct].
Since this is so, the connection is: "Therefore, listen to the knowledge of the ritual as it has been declared in the Tantra."
"It is difficult to find in the three worlds" is indeed according to the literal meaning, namely in heaven, the mortal world, and the netherworld (pātāla).
Alternatively, "in the three worlds" refers to the three worlds beginning with Vīra; the connection [of the sentence] is that the knowledge of the ritual exists within them.
"Abiding in the beginning, middle, and end" means abiding in mind, speech, and body;
or alternatively, it is said that this refers to the knowledge of the ritual because of the state of universal equal flavor (*samarasa*).

Regarding the phrase "the union of the churned and the churning": the "churned" (manthyā) refers to all the ḍākinīs, such as Vajravārāhī and others; the "churning" (manthānā) refers to all the heroes (vīras), beginning with the Blessed One. That ritual knowledge which possesses union with them is described in that way.
"Yathā tathā" means "in whatever manner," that is, in whatever way it is joined with mantra-recitation, meditation, and so forth.
"And yoga as well" means not only such knowledge of the ritual procedure, but also yoga within the tantra.
The connection is as follows: "Listen here in this tantra to all that has been declared in the *Khasama-tantra*";
for this very reason, it is said to be difficult to obtain.
By the word "etcetera" (ādi), the implements such as the mandala, fire-oblations, and external medicinal herbs are included.
By the word "yoga," the various specific yogas taught in the sections on subjugation (*vaśya*) and so forth are here being described.
"Listen"—some say that the Blessed One spoke thus to the Bhaṭṭārikā;
others maintain that it is appropriate for both to speak with a single voice;
still others hold that the Blessed Lady is the teacher and spoke thus to the Blessed One.
For this very reason, he will later state in the *Catuḥpūjā* that "O Great Hero" is an address to the Blessed One.

Now, regarding the procedure for the unsurpassed worship during the state of emission (*kṣaraṇāvasthā*) at the conclusion of the sequence of the churned and the churning, he says "the middle," and so forth.

Because it exists in the center, it is called the "middle" lotus; in that [lotus] is the supreme exhalation, which is the placement of the tongue. By what kind of [exhalation]? Namely, by that which is accompanied by scented water.
The meaning is: "precisely together with the thought of awakening" (bodhicitta).
“Kulikā” is the *samayabhāṣā* (conventional terminology) in the Tantra; it means that one should worship an external woman who is the very embodiment of Vajravārāhī.
The meaning is that one should act in such a way that satisfaction arises.
"At the time" means at the moment immediately following [the previous one].
"Specifically" means that this is a specific [moment] due to the striking of the vajra and lotus; such is the meaning.
The word "tu" (but/however) has the sense of "because."
Since the messengers are innate, perfected beings who are inferior, superior, or middling, one should therefore accomplish the attainment of desires with an internalized mind.
This is the intended meaning:
one should mentally effect the gratification of all external women who are directly situated within the three wheels.
From the phrase "with the drops of one's own semen" up to the end, "by means of recitation and meditation," it is easy to understand because it corresponds exactly to its literal sense.
One should always protect the deity of the pledge; the meaning is that one should never cause her harm at any time.
"The practitioner is well-composed" means that the practitioner must always be one whose mind is focused solely on the practice of yoga.

"Because success is not attained in the initiation mandala through a distinction among the *samayas*. The word *samaya* refers both to that which is to be protected and that which is to be consumed; it denotes the deities and the yogins who follow them. For "initiation" (*dīkṣā*) is merely an illustration.
The rest is easy to understand.
[1.15] Now, he shows the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*) with the words beginning with "honey" (*madhu*).
"Honey" refers to semen;
"blood" refers to blood;
"with camphor" means accompanied by human flesh.
Furthermore, the mention of "red" refers to urine;
"sandalwood" refers to feces.
*Raktacandanam* (red sandalwood) forms a *dvandva* compound;
the term *yojitam* (joined) forms a *samāsa* (compound) with these two.
In the midst of the assembly, in the center of the triple wheel; or else, in the midst of the samaya of those who maintain the single yoga.
The meaning is that it is to be established as something to be practiced.
The word "tu" (but/however) excludes connection with anything else.

And all those vajras are the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones; their *aṅka* is their mark (*cihna*) and their commitment (*samaya*). Furthermore, by the word "mark," it refers to the lotus vessel and the great conch shell.
Because he maintains that [vajra], he is the bearer of the marks and signs of all vajras.
This is the qualification of the five nectars.
"By means of the mouths of the ring finger and the thumb" means that one should lick [it] with the thumb and the ring finger.
"One who knows yoga" means a practitioner who maintains the divine yoga; that is to say, a mantra-master.

The phrase "like the drinking of soma" means that it is not to be drunk like liquor (surā); rather, the intention is that it is like the way Brahmins partake of the drink at the time of sacrifice because of its extreme purity.

A practitioner who has become thus attains eternal accomplishment (*siddhi*); the rest, beginning with "eternal," is easy to understand. Regarding "in the fourfold worship": this refers to external, secret, mental, and internal worship.
Alternatively, there are the Mahāmudrā, Samayamudrā, Dharmamudrā, and Karmamudrā; worship by means of these four is "fourfold worship.
Likewise, it occurs when one has entered into the union of the two organs.
"O Hero" is an address to the Blessed One.
*Tattvadhṛg* means one who maintains the reality, or alternatively, *tattva* means non-duality (*ananyatva*).

Therefore, together with all those who abide in the three wheels (*tricakra*), he maintains the state of equal single flavor (*samaikarasa*); having condensed and unified divine and human bliss, the Blessed One is the *vajra*, and because he maintains those [beings], he is the *yogin* known as *Vajradhṛk*.

"Sixteen parts are not worth even one-sixteenth part"—the meaning is that for a yogin of such a nature, those who possess other forms of yoga do not equal, that is, do not attain, even a single sixteenth part of him.
[1.18] Now, in order to describe the place where the mandala is to be drawn, he says "on a mountain," and so forth, ending with "one should practice in a cremation ground.
The meaning is that wherever one draws the mandala, there one should visualize the form of a great cremation ground.
With the words "city charcoal," and so forth, he describes the consecration of the dust (*rajaḥ-saṃskāra*).
"Possessing all characteristics" means being endowed with the characteristics of a master (*ācārya*).
"Right knowledge" refers to that which has arisen as a manifestation.

"Tantrajña" means one who knows the meaning of all tantras; or alternatively, it means one who is joined with the striking together of the vajra and lotus, that is to say, one who is engaged in bestowing the secret initiation.
"One who knows the mantra of Śrī Heruka" means one who has performed prior service and is free from doubt.
By the words beginning with "without anger," the characteristics of a teacher have been described.
By the [verse] beginning with "kapāla," according to the principle that a characteristic applied to a component becomes a qualifier of the whole,
the Great Seal (mahāmudrā) is said to be endowed with six seals.
By the phrase "with hair severed in a single lock," the garland of skulls above the forehead is indicated;
by this very same expression, the supreme single-piece lotus vessel is also described.

In all tantras, the characteristics of Mahāmudrā and so forth are taught through various methods of yoga; therefore, the wise person should practice them in their entirety and in the proper sequence according to the guru’s oral instructions.
For this very reason, it is said: "Having made oneself Śrī Heruka."
"One should then recollect Heruka" means that one should perform the ritual placement (vinyāsa) within the maṇḍala;
for this very reason, it is said that "one should place [him] in the heart of the wheel."
Having thus armed oneself, one should arm one's own body.

One should assign the walls according to the directions; that is to say, after the recitation of the *āli* and *kāli* samayas, one should subsequently assign the wall of hatred (*dveṣa-prākāra*), the wall of passion (*rāga-prākāra*), and the wall of delusion (*moha-prākāra*). Later, at the time when the peaked pavilion (*kūṭāgāra*) and so forth are completed, one should assign the vajra-wall (*vajra-prākāra*), the lotus-wall (*padma-prākāra*), and the wheel-wall (*cakra-prākāra*); such is the intended meaning.

Having thus armored oneself, one should indeed direct the weapon downward; that is to say, one should imagine the ground as consisting of diamond (vajra) as far as the limits of the netherworld (rasātala).
Regarding the "wheel-weapon": one should likewise armor oneself, situated within the wheel, with the lattices of weapons.
"But above, a lattice of arrows" means that one should place a lattice of arrows—a vajra-fence—above.
Furthermore, the meaning is that after the entry of the *jñānasattva* into oneself, one should fashion the inner palace (*kūṭāgāra*) and so forth, such as the cage (*pañjara*).
With the words "Thus," and so forth, he demonstrates the fearlessness of the mantra-practitioner who draws the mandala.
"Adorned with mudrās and mantras" means accompanied by a well-trained, refined external consort.
"Ālikhet" (one should draw) and so forth is easy to understand.
With the words "tataḥ" (then) and so forth, he indicates the mandala-line.
"Eight cubits" is intended as an illustrative indication.
"One should mark off double [the length]" means that one should mark off a long cord that is double the length of the mandala; this is the intended meaning.
"One should sacrifice" means one should worship, or rather, a sacrificial rite (yāga) should be performed.
"Ḍākinījālasaṃvara" means all those established within the three wheels.
Regarding the phrase "in its center" and so forth, it is exactly according to the literal meaning.
With the words beginning with "ojaskam," he elaborates upon the characteristics of Mahāmudrā.
"Ojaskam" means "possessing splendor."
"Flaming" means "possessing rays."
The remainder is exactly as it appears in the source text.

Regarding "vajrasambhinnasabhruvam": *sabhruvau* means "two eyebrows that are equal" (*samāne bhruvau*). The compound is analyzed as "one whose two eyebrows are properly split (*samyag bhinne*) like a vajra.
Alternatively, the meaning is "one whose eyebrows are split (*bhinnaṃ sabhruvam*) up to the extent of the vajra-garland above the forehead."
"Adorned with a hundred and fifty garlands" means adorned with a garland of fifty human heads from which blood flows.
With the words "In front of him," etc., he reveals the Blessed Lady Vajravārāhī.

Regarding the phrase "facing Mahābhairava," some interpret this as facing Maheśvara; however, that is entirely untenable, because [the subject] is not under discussion here, as the context concerns the Mahāmudrā of Vajravārāhī.
Therefore, the meaning is as follows: [she is] facing the Blessed One Mahābhairava, having embraced him with body, speech, and mind; the word *tu* (but/however) serves to emphasize that very point.
The remainder is easy to understand.
By the words "in the cardinal and intermediate directions," it means that one should worship the Kākāsyā and others.
By the phrase beginning with "and the jars" (*kalaśāṃś ca*), the characteristics of the jars are stated merely as a partial illustration.
They were endowed with such characteristics as being out of season, having large bellies, hanging lips, and long necks.
By the words "with pearls" and so forth, the five jewels are indicated.
"By copper vessels" is an adjective qualifying the jars.
The remainder is easy to understand.
If they are not obtained, there are nine vases;

however, if they are obtained, there are twenty-five vases: four for Lāma and the others, eight for Kākāsyā and the others, and two for the Sarvakarmika and Vijaya vases; thus, all together there are thirty-nine.
The meaning is that one should scatter the jewels as they have been obtained—beginning with silver and so forth—upon the maṇḍala according to their aesthetic beauty.
And one should worship the beautiful city; success is indeed certain, without a doubt—such [statements] are easily understood.
"Having consecrated oneself with scented water" means that one should consecrate oneself with "vajra-water," which is purified by mantra and mixed with fragrance.
"Facing all directions" is an epithet of the self;
it refers to the self as having the nature of Śrī Heruka, because the Blessed One has four faces.
"One should offer a hundred lamps" is indeed according to the literal meaning;

or else, specific varieties of diverse kinds are being stated, since elsewhere there is mention of "five lamps," whereas here there is the inclusion of the flesh of elephants, horses, and so forth. [2.8]
"One should mentally place all the ḍākinīs in the space above" means that they are established in the *cittacakra*, because the nature of the mind is to travel through space.

"Those ḍākinīs who are in the world of earth (bhūloka), one should place them everywhere in the maṇḍala"—that is, in every way, within that which is the speech-wheel (vākcakra) in the maṇḍala; "earth" (bhūḥ) means the ground (pṛthivī)—one should place those who move upon it, because [the speech-wheel] is situated in the center of the speech-wheel.
Furthermore, it is understood from the context that those residing in the netherworld (pātāla) should be placed in the body wheel (kāyacakra).

Regarding the phrase "the Mothers in the directions," at the four gates, one should place in due order the four: Kākāsyā, Ulūkāsyā, Śvānāsyā, and Śūkarāsyā. And as for the instruction "one should assign them to the intermediate directions," in that sequence, one places the four: Yamadāḍhī, Yamadūtī, Yamadaṃṣṭriṇī, and Yamamathanī.
Such is the sequence of arrangement.
By the words "with flowers" and so forth, the procedure for the fivefold offerings is shown.
Since it was already stated previously that "one should offer a hundred lamps," what is said here is for the purpose of completing the fivefold offerings (pañcopacāra).
It has not been explained [further] by the passage beginning with "one should worship," because its meaning is already established as it stands.
"One should act with full concentration" means, in every ritual procedure of worship, that one should be a knower of purity.
By the words "the preceptor" and so forth, the meaning is those who are present within the mandala; these are the preceptors.
By the words "according to one's ability" and so forth, he demonstrates the worship of the guru.
By the words beginning with "the bell," that which is to be performed by the principal and other preceptors has been stated.
By the passage beginning with "the small drum" (*paṭahikā*) and so forth, the procedure for the twentyfold worship is taught.
Up until the conclusion, "one should point out his family," it is quite easy to understand.

Immediately thereafter, having completed the entire consecration according to the procedure well-known from other tantras, he now indicates the secret consecration by means of the passage beginning with "one should worship the mudrā," since the primary focus here is the procedure for the secret consecration.

"One's own mudrā" means an external woman who is well-trained in mantra and tantra, endowed with the commitments (samaya) regarding what is to be protected and what is to be consumed; that is to say, a *samayinī*.

Having firmly established oneself as "well-composed" through the yoga of Śrī Heruka, and having emanated the consort through the yoga of Vajravārāhī, and having armored her with the great armor and so forth—and likewise having done so for the disciple—on the second day, one should again worship the maṇḍala, perform the consecration and other rites, arrange a comfortable bed such as a wooden plank, cloth, or mattress either in the center of the maṇḍala or near it, and then begin the secret initiation.

"One should apply a *tilaka* with blood over which [the mantra] has been recited three times. This means that when an external consort (*bāhyāṅganā*) endowed with the previously mentioned characteristics becomes menstruating (*puṣpavatī*), one should cause joy to arise through her by means of the sequence beginning with the drinking of soma and so forth; likewise, through the practice of striking the *vajra* and *padma*, at the moment of emission, one should perform the recitation of the Heart, Upahr̥daya, and Mālā-mantras for the disciple whose face is covered with a cloth, and bestow the consecration with the *vajra* and *padma* upon the seven locations: the head, the forehead, the two eyes, the mouth, the throat, and the heart.
The disciple, too, should taste it as if it were nectar placed upon his tongue.
Immediately after that, having opened his mouth, he should show the mandala.
Then, that which is the station of a deity for each [person] is the station for the secret initiation.
"In that regard, one should show her" means that one should show an external woman who is capable of bestowing the consecration.
"Correctly" means with a non-conceptual mind, because the disciple must likewise begin in that very manner.

Then, having prostrated before the city together with the preceptor, and having performed a circumambulation, the disciple should then proceed counter-clockwise for the commencement. Having prostrated to the mandala and the preceptor according to the rule—meaning, having begun according to the same procedure by which the preceptor bestowed the initiation upon the disciple—the intention is that the goal must be accomplished by that disciple toward the preceptor in that very same way. (p. 115)
Then, the passage beginning with "tatas tu" and so forth is easy to understand because it accords with the actual meaning.
"All that resides in Śrī Heruka" means that it resides in the yogi who maintains the yoga of Śrī Heruka.
Then, regarding the statement "the ḍākinīs cause the worlds to expand," the individual names of the ḍākinīs established within the three wheels are now stated.
By the passage beginning with "mahāvīryā" and so forth, it is stated in reverse order.

[4.1] Thus, in all cases, by means of pronouncing their own names and so forth, there are sixty mantras for the twenty-four ḍākinīs, the heroes, the four starting with Ḍākinī, and the eight starting with Kākāsyā; these are joined with the syllable *oṃ* at the beginning and ending with *hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ*.
This is because it has been shown that "all are illuminated by the syllable *oṃ*. [4.2]

"Having seen the supreme and most excellent yoga, [one regards] another as worthless wood-worm"—this means that having seen this supreme yoga of Śrī Heruka, one regards another as being like worthless straw, a specific kind of grass, or as being devoid of essence like a wood-worm.

With the words "bestowers of accomplishment" (*siddhidā*) and so forth, he describes the power of the yogin who has thus become perfected. Precisely because they have attained accomplishment, they fulfill all desires;
that is, he becomes capable of bestowing whatever objects are desired.
"Having attained heroism" means that one possesses the heroic prowess existing within the three wheels.
"Having seen the mandala in the house" means having seen the mandala drawn in the mandala-house.
Merely by the completion of the rite of initiation (*abhiṣeka*), these aforementioned qualities become accomplished;
how much more so, then, through the power of constant practice such as recitation (*japa*) and meditation (*dhyāna*)?
In order to demonstrate the greatness of the tantra, he says: "Then, having known [this], one should meditate constantly.
Thus, the fruit of the tantra has been stated.
"Just as the word of the Tathāgata" means that because the Blessed Buddha speaks without error, the authority of the tantra has been stated.
Now, with the words "herein are the mantra-syllables," he demonstrates the procedure for extracting the root mantra of the Blessed Śrī Heruka.
"Having made the vowels and consonants equal" means that one should draw the letters such that the syllables are not uneven.
"Transformed from the groups" means that, first of all, the consonant-syllables of the mantra must be extracted.
The meaning is that there are eight mantra-words, namely "catuś-catuḥ-vijñeyam."
"O best of sages, regarding the *prastara*," the meaning is that there are seven groups [of consonants], beginning with the letter *ka* and ending with the letter *ha*.
"One should extract the Hero situated there"—because the location and the one who locates it are of a single form, the word "Hero" (vīra) refers to the mantra.
"Accomplishing all desires and aims" describes the power of that mantra.
"The fifth of the fourth" refers to the letter *na*.
The fifth of the fifth is the letter *ma*.
The fourth of the fifth [group] is the letter *bha*.
"The third of the first" refers to the letter *ga*.
In the twenty-ninth [position], one should place the letter *va*.
The "first" of the fourth [varga] refers to the letter *ta*.
The fourth of the semivowels (antasthā) is indeed the letter *va*.
The second [syllable] of that very [word] is the letter *ra*.
The thirtieth, however, is the letter Śa.
The twenty-sixth is the letter *ya*.
"Half of half of a hundred" refers to the letter *ma*.
The thirty-third is the letter *ha*.
The first [syllable] of the first [group] is the letter *ka*.
"The third of the semivowels" refers to the letter *l*.
The third of the first [group] is the letter *ga*.
And the letter *sa* is indeed the thirty-second.
The fifth [syllable] of the fourth [line] is the letter *na*.
The fourth [syllable] of the fifth [group], namely the letter *bha*.
The letter *y* is that which is first among the semivowels (*antastha*).
The third [consonant] of the second [varga] is the letter ja.
The first letter of the third [group] is the syllable *ṭa*.
The fifth of the fifth is the letter *ma*.
"The first of the first" refers to the letter *ka*.
Likewise, the eleventh is the letter *ṭa*.
And the sixteenth is the letter *ta*.
"The first of the third" refers to the letter ṭa.
The twenty-sixth is the letter *ya*.
The third of the fourth [group] is the letter *da*.
The second of the *ūṣman* sounds is the letter *ṣ*.
The first [syllable] of the first [section] is the letter *ka*.
The twenty-seventh is the letter *ra*.
The twenty-eighth is the letter *la*.
But the third of the first [group] is the letter *ga*.
The thirty-first is the letter *ṣa*.
And the fifteenth is indeed the letter ṇa.
The twenty-fifth is the letter *ma*.
The second [syllable] of the first [group] is the letter *kha*.
The twenty-sixth is the letter ya.
The thirty-second is the letter *sa*.
The letter *ha* is at the end of the sibilants (*ūṣman*).
Furthermore, the thirty-second is indeed the letter *sa* itself.
The fourth letter of the fifth group is the syllable *bha*.
The third [letter] of the second [group] is the letter ja.
The fourth letter of the fifth group is the syllable *bha*.
The third of the sibilants (ūṣman) is the letter sa.
The twenty-seventh is the letter *ra*.
Among the semi-vowels (antasthā), the first is the letter ya.
The twenty-first section.
The second of the antaḥsthās is the letter *repha*.
The thirtieth is the letter Śa.
The first [syllable] of the fifth [group] is the letter *pa*.
The first of the *uṣman* sounds is the letter *ś*.
Likewise, by the specific indication of the form "dy," the seed-syllable of the Blessed One’s Dharma-seal is stated.
The first [syllable] of the fourth [quarter] is the letter *ta*.
But that which is the first of the *ūṣman* sounds is the letter *ś*.
The twenty-eighth is the letter *la*.
The second [syllable] of the first [group] is the letter *kha*.
The first [syllable] of the third [line] is the letter ṬA.
The third [syllable] of the first [group] is the letter *ga*.
The fourth [letter] of the fourth [group], the letter *dh*, is the fourth [syllable].
The second [consonant] of the semi-vowels (antasthā) is the letter *ra*.
The fifth letter of the third [varga] is the letter ṇa.
The utterance of the essential form of the Vyākaraṇa reveals the seed-syllable of the Blessed One’s Dharma-seal.
The fourth letter of the first [varga] is the letter *gh*.
The eighth syllable is the letter *ja*.
The fifth letter, *na*, belongs to the fourth [vowel].
The fifth of the fifth is the letter *ma*.
"Twenty-seven" refers to the letter *ra*.
The fourth of the fourth is the letter *dh*.
The twenty-seventh is indeed the letter *ra*.
The twenty-sixth is the letter ya.
The twenty-fifth is the letter *ma*.
The letter *ha* is the thirty-third.
The fourth [syllable] of the fourth [group] is the letter *dh*.
The fifth of the fifth is the letter *ma*.
The fifth letter of the fourth [varga] is the letter *na*.
The first [syllable] of the first [group] is the letter *ka*.
The twenty-seventh is the letter *ra*.
The fourth letter among the semivowels (antasthā) is the letter *va*.
The twenty-first type.
The second of the sibilants (ūṣman) is the letter ṣa.
And "twenty-six" refers to the letter *ya*.
Regarding "of the Vidyārāja": "vidyās" are the ḍākinīs who are sovereigns of the three wheels; their king is the Vidyārāja.
The meaning is "his mantra."
The meaning is that he is accomplished merely by reciting the words "devoid of all means of accomplishment."
The remainder is easy to understand.
With the words "and the *y*-group," etc., he extracts the heart-mantras of the six heroes who constitute the armor.
The eighth seed-syllable from the *ya*-group is the letter *ha*.
Likewise, one should place the seed-syllables of the letter *ha*, adorned with twelve vowels excluding the neuter ones: *ha, hā, hi, hī, hu, hū, he, hai, ho, hau, haṃ, haḥ*.
"Having interposed other syllables" means having omitted the second, fourth, sixth, eighth, tenth, and twelfth [syllables].

"The six-limbed Śrī Heruka is proclaimed" means the six limbs of Heruka; this is due to the metaphorical treatment of the support and the supported as non-different, or because they are so in the ultimate sense.
"Union with the six heroes" refers to the unions of the six heroes, beginning with Oṃ.
"Established in each individual syllable" means that one should place the syllable *oṃ* before the letter *ha*.
The meaning is that those mantras are armor-mantras (*kavaca*).

The meaning is that these heart-mantras are to be known by the practitioner as being joined with the syllables *oṃ*, *namaḥ*, *svāhā*, *vauṣaṭ*, *hūṃ* (twice), and *phaṭ*. Thus, they are to be understood by the practitioner (*sādhaka*).
First, regarding "the heart as well," by means of this *oṃ ha*, Vajrasattva [is placed] in the heart.
But the second head is remembered as "Namaḥ" and "Hi"; by means of this, one should place Vairocana on the head.
For the third, one should bestow the crest-lock (śikhā) with the mantra "svāhā hu"; by this, Padmanarteśvara is placed upon the crest-lock.
"The fourth shall be the armor"—thus, by means of this "vauṣaṭ" in the form of armor, Śrī Heruka [is placed] upon the two shoulders.
The fifth, however, becomes the eye; with "hūṃ 2 ho," Vajrasūrya is placed in the two eyes.
"The weapon of the sixth is now declared": by means of *phaṭ haṃ*, Hayagrīva’s weapon for all limbs is established.
"By the thirteenth of the vowels" means that one should join the second syllable of the mantra with the thirteenth vowel, the letter *o*.
"Joined with the eleventh vowel and adorned with the sixth syllable" means that one should join the letter *e* (ekāra) with the sixth syllable of the mantra.
"Joined with the fourth of the vowels" means that one should join the seventh syllable of the mantra with the vowel *ī*.
The meaning is that one should join the eighth syllable, which is conjoined with the eleventh vowel, with the letter *e*.
"But the ninth [syllable] is adorned by the second of the vowels"—the meaning is that one should join the ninth syllable with the letter *Ā*.
The meaning is that one should join the twelve-syllable [mantra] with the letter Ā, by means of the second of the vowels.

Then one should give the twenty-first [consonant], conjoined with the second vowel, as the fourteenth syllable; the meaning is that one should join the fourteenth syllable with the letter *pa*, and then join that very same [letter] with the vowel *ā*.

The meaning is that one should take the twentieth syllable, join it with the third vowel, and thus form the fifteenth syllable; having joined it with the letter *na*, one should then conjoin it with the third vowel.
"Joined with the fifteenth vowel" means that one should join the anusvāra to the sixteenth syllable.
"Joined with the third vowel, it is considered beautiful and supreme; [it is] seventeen syllables"—the meaning is that one should join the seventeen-syllable mantra with the vowel *i*.
"Joined with the second vowel, the eighteenth [letter] is supremely beneficial"—this is indeed easy to understand.

The twenty-one syllable [mantra] joined with the second of the vowels, the twenty-three syllable [mantra] joined with the fifth of the *mātṛkās*, and the twenty-four syllable [mantra] joined with the thirteenth of the vowels—all of this is easily accomplished.
"Taking the first of the classes, conjoined with twenty-five syllables" means that one should join the letter *ka* to the root of the twenty-five syllables.

Regarding the first [syllable] of the third [group], "the twenty-sixth letter, differentiated by the second vowel"—this means one should join it with the second vowel. And regarding "the twenty-eighth itself, honored by the fifteenth," this means that an *anusvāra* should be placed upon the letter *da*.

The first [letter] of the third [group] joined with its lower part, likewise joined with fire—that is, having joined the letter *ṭ* at its base with the letter *r*, and joined it with the second vowel—that is, with the letter *ā*, the twenty-ninth syllable becomes the form *ṣṭrā*.
The meaning is that one should join it to the base of the letter *ṣ*.
The remainder is indeed easy to understand.
"Bhāskara" is the designation for the letter *ra*.
The remainder is according to the literal meaning.
"Dahana" is the technical name for the letter *ra*.
"Cāliṃśa" means "forty."
The remainder is easy to understand according to all the tantras.
This mantra, "The Heart that Afflicts the Ḍākinīs," causes all terrifying ḍākinīs and others to fall into a state of terror as soon as it is uttered.
Beginning with *oṃ* and ending with *hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ*, this is indeed easy to understand.

One's own self (*svam ātmānam*) is the *Sarvavīrasamāyogaḍākinījālasaṃvara*; even though the mantra is of the nature of Śrī Heruka, its meaning is that it is established within the three wheels (*tricakra*) and is the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of all ḍākas and ḍākinīs.
By means of the sequence beginning with *svāhā* and proceeding in reverse order, the twenty-two-syllable heart mantra is presented;
it should be understood as: *oṃ śrīvajra he he ru ru kaṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ ḍākinījālasaṃvaraṃ svāhā*.
In the same manner, the heart mantras of the six yoginīs are also stated in reverse order.
Then, "oṃ hāṃ hrīṃ hreṃ hūṃ phaṭ" is to be understood [as the mantra].
Regarding the passage beginning with "vaṃkāre," this is the meaning:

one should join the syllable *oṃ* before the syllable *vaṃ*; the syllable *hāṃ* before the syllable *yoṃ*; the syllable *hrīṃ* before the syllable *moṃ*; the syllable *hreṃ* before the syllable *hrīṃ*; the syllable *hūṃ* before the syllable *hūṃ*; and the syllable *phaṭ* before the syllable *phaṭ*. This is the connection [of the words].
Oṃ vaṃ Vajravārāhī at the navel; hāṃ yoṃ Yāminī at the heart;
hrīṃ moṃ Mohanī at the face.
Hreṃ Hrīṃ Saṃcālanī on the head;
Hūṃ Hūṃ Saṃtrāsanī on the crest-lock;
Phaṭ Phaṭ Caṇḍikā, in the form of a weapon, on all limbs.
The heart-mantra of the six yoginīs:
Oṃ vajravairocanīye svāhā. This is the near-heart-mantra of the Blessed Lady.
It describes the majesty of the mantra: "The great vidyā of the ḍākinīs has not existed, nor will it ever exist.
On this earth, among the four jewels, the mantra-garland is supreme; the ḍākinī is the great vidyā, and the King of Vidyās is Śrī Heruka.
Thus, within the maṇḍala of the earth, regarding the tantras and mantras taught by oneself and others.
The four mantras are indeed the four jewels:
the mantra-garland of the Blessed One and the Blessed Lady, as well as the heart-mantra, the near-heart-mantra, and the armor-mantra.
In the tantra, for the sake of removing all confusion, the case-endings have been assigned according to preference.
It should be inferred according to the sense of that [context].
Alternatively, "the four jewels" refers to both the *hṛdaya* and the *upahṛdaya*.
Alternatively, there is another meaning:
the reference is specifically to the root mantra of the Blessed One, because that alone is the subject under discussion.
"Catura" means clever, dexterous, or—in other words—capable.
The yogin performs all that which has been instructed [by the teacher].
For this very reason, they are called "jewels" (*ratna*); the garland of mantras is like a jewel because it bestows desired objects, just like a wish-fulfilling gem (*cintāmaṇi*).
Thus, the connection is with the phrase "the garland of mantras of the Bhagavatī."
For this very reason, its efficacy is stated by the words "the ritual activity of the Vidyārāja," and so forth.
"Of the Vidyārāja" is a designation for the *mālāmantra* or the *mūlamantra*.
The connection is as follows: "I shall explain the application of the rituals for that mantra which was first indicated in due order and according to the rule."
The passage beginning with "trailokya" and so forth is easy to understand.
The repetition of the phrase "all the origins of the gods" is for the sake of clarifying the meaning of the accomplishment (*siddhi*), since there is no fault of tautology in all the tantras.

"Terrifying the clouds," and so forth: first, it is understood according to its literal meaning; subsequently, this is the intended sense—during the state of union of the vajra and the lotus, he terrifies the clouds and brings the ḍākinīs under his control.
He causes it to rain by means of the stream of water that is the thought of awakening.
He restrains and establishes [them]; they exist together with women and mudrās.
It dries up those oceans and brings them to a state of exhaustion.
It brings down the riverbank and causes a light pearl oyster shell to become fixed.
He restrains Indra; being enraged, he causes another's faculty to fail.
He causes the earth to tremble, and he causes all the sources of phenomena (*dharmodayā*) to tremble in a spirit of competitive emulation.
Having climbed a tree, one goes wherever one desires; having mounted the yantra together with the vidyā, one becomes a traveler through the sky.
It steals all mantras; whatever secret is given by anyone whatsoever in their own place within the three worlds, he, mounted upon all the yantras, speaks thus.
"It takes away all accomplishments" means that it seizes and brings forth those accomplishments associated with the vidyādharas and others who possess all siddhis.
It draws out blood; it draws forth a woman connected to a king who possesses many protective marks.
"He dismisses again" means that he places [the object] back in its own place once more.

Thinking, "I shall manifest many thousands of forms," for the sake of performing the welfare of all sentient beings, he emits from his own body—conjoined with wisdom and skillful means—forms that pervade the entire expanse of space.
"It is seen by will; it is not seen by will" means "by the will of the gods."

It pulverizes palaces, tree-tops, and so forth. Here, "palace" (*prāsāda*) refers to the lotus because it is the abode of all Buddhas; "tree" (*druma*) refers to the vajra because it is the male principle; and "top" (*śikhara*) refers to the nose of the goddess Padmanāsā. The meaning is that, according to one's desire—whether mild, moderate, or intense—one strikes mercilessly when clashing the vajra and the lotus.
The meaning is that it makes poison into nectar; that is, one should enjoy the sense objects as if they were nectar.
"It makes nectar into poison" means that it treats the object of sense like poison, as if it were nectar; the meaning is that one does not form an attachment to it.
The statement "he makes the *soma* into milk" means that he drinks the *bodhicitta* as if it were milk.
The phrase "he makes the milk into Soma" means that he causes the milk to taste like water; the sense is that one should cause it to taste like the drinking of Soma.
"It takes away all odors" means that it removes those odors by means of the five nectars (pañcāmṛta).
Wherever he desires, there he transfers it; he transfers that fragrance elsewhere, such as into the food of Brahmins and others.
Therefore, in order to clarify this very preceding point, he says "with the face" and so forth:
"with the face [like] the king of Garuḍas" refers to the movement of the vehicle;
"the creator of emanation" means that the Garuḍa, eager for flight, raises both wings.
In the same way, he performs the union with the women; the meaning is that having taken the *bodhicitta* with his mouth, it is to be placed in the mouth of the goddess.

"The best of men" means that the man who practices in this manner becomes the most excellent in the three worlds. In that state, the fortune (*lakṣmī*) held in his hand cannot be thwarted by anyone; the meaning is that the miraculous transformations (*vikurvaṇa*) of such a yogin according to his will cannot be obstructed even by all the Victors (*jināḥ*).
Beginning with the words "In this way," it is indeed according to the reality, because that [state] abides at the limit of excellence.
Regarding the phrase "with the charcoal from a cemetery," the instruction is stated here:

having cut a branch of a *vibhītaka* tree facing south with the axe of a *caṇḍāla* or similar tool on the night of the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, one should burn it in a cemetery, extinguish it with donkey urine, and collect those coals and ashes, storing them properly. Thereafter, the rites taught in the tantra should be performed; their result will be unimpeded.

Regarding the phrase "with an *atimuktaka* creeper," this is the instruction: during a lunar eclipse, the practitioner who has recited the mantra one hundred thousand times should sit upon a pavilion made of *atimuktaka* creepers. Having performed the protective rites and so forth, he should dye a thread spun by a virgin red, wrap it around a staff situated toward the western direction, and then—naked and with hair disheveled—the practitioner, holding that staff with his left hand from the moment of the eclipse's onset until its end, should recite the mantra continuously. Subsequently, having cut [the creeper] with a weapon according to the prescribed ritual, [he should use] the tip and the root.
One should observe this: it moves forward by the tip and returns by the root.
The remainder is exactly as it is in reality.
By the words "food and drink," etc., it is stated that the practitioner's requirements are easily obtained everywhere.
(p. 122) By the words "Dharma," etc., the establishment of the practitioner’s three bodies is explained. In this regard, the instruction is as follows:

the state established in the three wheels arisen from a single *hūṃ* syllable is the *dharmakāya*. Having withdrawn all [deities] into a single body and armored them with the great armors, the state of recitation (*jāpa*) is the *saṃbhogakāya*. Immediately thereafter, in the heart...

The state of the expansion and withdrawal of the *ālikāli* together with the moon is the *nirmāṇakāya*. "He attains the enjoyment of gnosis" means that the enjoyment (*saṃbhoga*) of gnosis is its experience; he attains that, meaning he becomes equal to Śrī Heruka.
The remainder is easy to understand.
With the words "of this mantra," etc., he explains the applications of the heart-mantra.
The heart is said to be the essence.
The remainder is exactly as it appears in the text.
By the passage beginning with "of which person," etc., the characteristics of the sacrificial animal are defined.
Some say that because he speaks the truth, his mind remains settled for a long time and does not depart quickly; others say that his eyes do not stare wildly for a long time nor close quickly.
The remainder is easy to understand.
With the passage beginning "on the sole of the foot of a dead human," etc., he explains the binding of pills for the purpose of making oneself invisible.
"Triloha" refers to gold, silver, and copper.
By the words "with the tip of the index finger," and so forth, he describes the extraction of blood.
In this regard, the procedure is as follows:

Having taken a human skull-cup and performed the preliminary service (*pūrvasevā*), the mantra-practitioner, instantly assuming the yoga of Vajrarudra, should—merely by the utterance of the syllable *HŪṂ*—emanate Khaṇḍarohā, holding a weapon in her hand, from within his own right nostril. With her, he should cause the piercing of the veins in five locations upon the victim’s head according to the victim's name, and he should visualize the skull-cup becoming completely filled with streams of that blood.

Then, for the sake of bringing [the victim] back, he should again, with his left hand, visualize that very threatening forefinger in a gentle and peaceful form, filling that same victim; thus the victim becomes restored to health. [l2.2]
By the words beginning with "having consecrated," the headache is made perfectly clear.
"One should fill the skull-cup" means with milk or wine, according to the context.
All the specific sequences of applications mentioned by "gorocanā" and so forth are indeed exactly as they appear in their literal meaning.
Because the capacity has arisen within the yogin:

if the power has not yet arisen, then having performed one hundred thousand recitations of the syllables with a concentrated mind according to the prescribed ritual, and having manifested Khaṇḍarohā, all rites should be performed with a mind absorbed in her.
Regarding the phrase "having recited it three times with one's own blood," the ellipsis to be supplied is "having placed it in the mouth.
One should gaze incessantly upon the desired object of yoga, such as a Yoginī, Lāmā, or Rūpiṇī, and so forth.
Nevertheless, he states that the application of the donkey is superior.
In this regard, the sequence of instruction is as follows:
one should draw the mandala for the purpose of initiation exactly as it is, extending outward to the limits of the Cakravāḍa mountains.
In the center of the filaments of an eight-petaled lotus there, the syllable *hūṃ* is surrounded by the vowels (*āli*) and consonants (*kāli*).
On the four petals of the directions are both the *hṛdaya* and the *upahṛdaya* mantras;
on the four petals of the corners are skull-cups filled with blood;
and on the twenty-four spokes are the forty-eight mantras beginning with Khaṇḍakapālin and the others.
Within the root sūtra are the eight mantras beginning with Kākāsyā.
Above the root sūtra, within the four gates, are the four lines of the Sumbha-Niṣumbha mantra in their respective order.
On both sides of the enclosure wall is the root mantra.
Outside the wall, on the top of the gate, at the joints of the eight turrets, and on both sides, are the armor-mantras;
and on the circular rim is the root mantra of the Blessed Lady.

Outside of that, having surrounded it with the forms of rays and the great armor-seeds such as Pullīra, Malaya, and so forth, one should fashion and place within the center of that wheel an image made of rice-flour in the shape of a donkey. Having anointed it with oil and lac, and having taken hold of the "donkey-yoga" characterized by a flowing-blooded mouth according to the sequence taught in the Tantra, one should light lamps in the four corners and, having previously performed the service, recite the desired mantra as spoken here without interruption; then one shall see the image there.
This is the instruction. [14.1]
"Having made an offering (bali) by that" means having consumed it.
Now, with the words "In all the vows," and so forth, he explains the syllable-ornaments (akṣaracchomaka).
In that regard, it is according to reality.
The designation "Ḍā" is to be understood from the context.
"Lāmayas tathā" means "I am born from the Lāmā family. This is the intended meaning.
"O pair of shanks, you must unite with him; this is the secret sign."

[15] The intention is that one should act according to the will of the deities, having deliberated upon one's own system and the systems of others, with the thought that "both what has been eaten and what has not been eaten must be offered.
Revealing this very same meaning once again, he says: "The systems of others..."
"Supreme" means most excellent;
for that very reason, it is "pleasing," which is to say agreeable to the mind.
The meaning "it should be given to the devotee" is made explicit by the word ending in the dative case.
Now, with the words "atha ata" and so forth, he demonstrates the characteristics of the deities' own systems and other systems;
all of this is easy to accomplish. [16.1] (p.124)
"Born into the family and lineage" means one who has entered the teaching of the Sugata.
"Followers of Vīrarudra" means they are born from the family (kula) of Śrī Heruka.
Vīramatī was embraced by Surāvairin.
Born from the Vajra family, she is born from the Vajravārāhī family.
She follows the lineage of the Tathāgata and is born from the family of Vairocana.
Furthermore, with the words "again, likewise these seven," and so forth, he explains the suitability of the practitioner for those aforementioned [deities].

Regarding the phrase "the syllables of the family-mantra (*kulavidyā*) are six letters": the *vidyā* of the family (*kula*)—that is, the deities who have become the practitioner’s companions—are represented as syllables because their intrinsic nature is indestructible; "they are six letters" means that they exist in six modes.
"Badhnāti" and so forth constitute the definition of the six syllables;
it is indeed easy to understand.
"But likewise, the yoginīs and the ḍākinīs are difficult to find" means that both the yoginīs and the ḍākinīs are rare.
The intention is that because they truly arise from the five nectars, they become easily attainable through the practice of the five nectars.
The characteristics of the seven [deities] beginning with Yāminī and the seven beginning with Rūpikā have been stated both collectively and individually;
by the mere thorough knowledge of which, they become attainable for the practitioner.
Their family mudrās are the skull-cup and so forth;
they are not five for each individually, but rather as one desires.
The wheel is *so le 'o*;
the vajra is *saṃtrāsanī*.
From "after this" (*ataḥ param*) and so forth, other specific characteristics are described.
Women endowed with the tallakṣaṇa are the yoginīs who are to be accomplished by the practitioner.
Following this, he says, "Next I shall explain the characteristics of the lāmās," and so forth, referring to the characteristics of women who are solitary lāmās.
Now, beginning with the words "atha" and so on, he speaks in order to show the *aṅgacchommakas*.
"One should show the Garuḍa" means that one brandishes—meaning one shakes or causes to tremble—the two arms, which are bent in the shape of wings with the index fingers extended.
"Maṇḍala" means the assembly of the pledge (samayamelāpaka).
From the words "from this point forward" and so forth, the mudrā and pratimudrā are prescribed.
"The middle one" refers to the middle finger.
The ring finger and the index finger.
"Paṭṭiśa" means in the form of a spear above the forehead.
Regarding the "spear" (śūla): by touching with the little finger and the thumb, one should display the remaining three fingers in the shape of a spear.
The term *sīma* refers to the upper portion in the middle of the head.
"Guhyakās" refers to the yoginīs.
Now, with the words "from this" and so forth, he demonstrates the unconventional secret signs (*cchommaka*) of the ḍākinīs.

"Of whomsoever"— meaning of whichever practitioner— "the devoted consort," that is, the external woman who is the deity, is under the sway of affection through her entire being and is unaware of any other man, for that hero, that yogin,
the whole earth becomes his object of enjoyment;
it does not belong to anyone else, such as a king or the like.

"Having made the earth the support, one should worship the vow of yoga"—the meaning is that having made the earth, the goddess well-trained in the independent mantras, the support, one should worship, that is, perform the ritual of, the "vow of yoga," which is the practice of Mahāmudrā.
Regarding the phrase "and the banner-attachment is born eternally": "banner" (*dhvaja*) refers to the *liṅga*, and the compound means "she whose attachment (*sakti*) is to that."
The "enclosure" (saṃpuṭa) is to be known by means of the mirror; thus, the meaning is that she who constantly gazes into the mirror must know—that is, must realize—the "flag-power" (dhvaja-śakti).
Now, with the words beginning "Potangī," he demonstrates various multi-syllabic secret signs (chommaka).

"The characteristics of the four groups" refers to the characteristics of the four—namely, the Yoginīs, the Lāmas, the Mudrās, and the Chommakas. Regarding the statement "the messengers are established in direct and reverse order," the meaning is that although Mahāvīryā and the others were previously indicated in reverse order, they should now be arranged in direct order; for this very reason, it is said: "They constantly bestow success in the upper and lower realms."
The meaning is that when those situated below are placed above, they then become bestowers of accomplishment (siddhi).

"She who grants all accomplishments"—this means that those female messengers (dūtīs) grant accomplishment through mere sight and touch; how much more so when they have been ritually mastered? Such is the meaning.

"Through kissing and embracing, especially on the yoga-pīṭhas—however many collections of yogas there are, they are remembered as bestowing all accomplishments"—herein the meaning is this: however many fields (kṣetra) and subordinate fields (upakṣetra) there are, which are yoga-pīṭhas, the female messengers (dūtīs) stationed therein grant accomplishment through kissing and embracing; "especially" means that this is particularly so.
The meaning of "it should be given," and so forth, is that upon seeing a *samayinī* or *yoginī*, one should offer edible foods, drinks, sacrificial porridge (*caru*), *chomma*-signs, and the like.

The meaning of the passage beginning with "mother" (*mātā*) and so forth is that when they become fit for instruction in mantra and tantra, one must then recognize mother and the others as being bound [to the practitioner].
Regarding the passage beginning with "yasya" (of whom): the meaning is that she to whom one gives the mantra becomes suitable for him, and no other.
With the passage beginning with "samaya" (the pledge), he explains what must be practiced by the yogin.
"Vāma," and so forth: whether it be a woman or a man, having seen a Yoginī, one should proceed by keeping her to one's left side.
By the words "it is known" and so forth, the meaning is that one should perform the left-handed practice even in a house or a field that is very far away.
"There is no yoga higher than Heruka" means that there is no other superior yoga apart from the yoga of Heruka.
For this very reason, the master is called the "mother of yoga"; the meaning is that the master who maintains that yoga stands in the place of a mother to all yogas.

"In this tantra, the practitioner and that which is truly good"—the connection is with the phrase "those who hold the yoga and have been consecrated in this tantra are not to be despised," and so forth.
Regarding the words "eight" and so on, the meaning is that they increase faith and devotion and become the cause of the accomplishments (*siddhis*).
How is that?
It is the observance of the previously mentioned commitments (samaya) such as the left-hand conduct;
this is the first.

"One who would go to union with another's wife through conceptualization of desire is greedy"—this means that he who, by means of conceptualizing desire or the wish for sensual pleasure, engages in union with another's wife is "greedy.
Therefore, there is the avoidance of such union with others.
This is the second [precept].
"One should become non-dual, devoid of the distinction between self and other"—
this is the third [verse].
"Unobstructed" (apratihata) means that it is not obstructed;
this is the fourth [point].

Regarding the phrase "one whose activity is the conduct of the pledges" (*samayācāraceṣṭita*): the "pledges" (*samaya*) are the goddesses; their "conduct" (*ācāra*) is their will; one whose "activity" (*ceṣṭā*), that is, whose exertion, lies therein is "one whose activity is the conduct of the pledges.
This is the fifth [type].

Regarding "sumanthāna" [in the phrase] "nārīśvaryā sumanthāna": at the time of striking the vajra-lotus in sumanthāna, the state of being devoid of sovereignty is not to be produced; rather, the meaning is that sovereignty alone is ordained.
This is the sixth [section].
"Brahmacarya and likewise meditation" means that at the time of the emission of the bodhicitta, one should practice—that is, observe—the reality of Brahmā;
this is the seventh [chapter].
"Absence of anger is the movement through the channels" means that at the time of receiving the bodhicitta, one must not harbor resentment.
The connection is that the eight supreme and most excellent commitments (samaya) are to be known by practitioners.
"Common to all tantras" means that this secret is common to all tantras;
for this very reason, those who know other tantras do not understand this intended secret.

Therefore, it has been stated that [the self] is not to be destroyed by reasons; the meaning is that it is not to be refuted—that is, it is not to be invalidated—by reasons, namely by the means of valid cognition such as direct perception and the rest.
Furthermore, as for what should be done, he says: "It is grasped by faith alone.
By the words "not with the hand," and so forth, he indicates that very same point.
"The wise one should move the little finger" means that at the time of worshipping the Goddess, one is possessed of the yoga of the deity.
Alternatively, if one who is well-trained in the mantras and tantras cannot be found, one should worship even another [woman] after making her extraordinary (*aprākṛta*).
The meaning is that at that time, for the wise yogin, all the messengers (dūtayaḥ) become perfectly gracious, as they are thus established.

Regarding the statement, "the man who is a worshipper, pure, an illuminator, and endowed with qualities," the man endowed with qualities—the yogin—is found to be of three kinds: the "worshipper" (ārādhaka) is one whose creative intuition (pratibhā) has not yet arisen; the "pure" (viśuddha) is one whose capacity has arisen; and the "illuminator" (dīpaka) is the intermediate illuminator, whose intuition has arisen to some extent and who awakens both himself and others to the goal.

Alternatively, the *ārādhaka* is one who propitiates the deity through the practice of mantra-yoga; the *guṇavān* is one who knows the meaning of the scriptures; and the *dīpaka* is one capable of performing the welfare of all sentient beings, like a lamp.

Regarding the phrase "in every village, wandering, his messengers possess the characteristics of form," the meaning is that the messengers (*dūtīs*) endowed with the characteristics of form belonging to each of these three types of yogins are seen in every village.
The messengers are like the edge of a sword; the meaning is that these messengers are as difficult to propitiate as the edge of a sword.
"Pavitram" and so forth; "pavitra" means those which increase merit.

"And the practitioner attains accomplishment" means that having obtained those [means], the practitioner attains the desired accomplishment. "From excellent contact," and so forth, is easy to understand. "The two means" means the means for accomplishing both mundane and supramundane accomplishments.

This shows the superiority [of this system] by stating that for one practicing for the sake of accomplishment (*siddhi*), there is indeed only one messenger (*dūtī*), meaning there is only one Śrī Heruka yoga. Alternatively, when someone is practicing for the sake of accomplishment, he possesses only one supreme yoga; then, by him, the messengers—the yoginīs—are impelled. Such is the connection [to be understood] in the context of the proximity of the means for achieving accomplishment.

"Attained through the lineage of gurus, consecrated, and well-restrained by the female messengers (dūtīs) who have spoken correctly"—the meaning is that when one has become well-restrained by the consecrations obtained through the lineage of gurus, then one is correctly addressed by the female messengers, the yoginīs.
"And one whose habit is the union with mudrās" means one whose habit is the union with external women;
"complete" means that at that time he becomes fully perfected.
"Born from the cause of gnosis" means that the Blessed One Vajrarudra is born from the cause—the causal condition—which is the culmination of the excellence of gnosis.
"Having risen in the morning" means having risen from one's bed at the end of the night.
The Blessed One is the Mahāmudrā yoga, the self of the mind.
Having performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa upon the form—that is, having armored the body with the armor-mantras beginning with the six heroes (ṣaḍvīra).
"One should employ weapons upon one's own limbs" means that one should cover the entire body with networks of weapons.
Having purified his body, he should constantly recite the mantra; thus, the practitioner of mantra, having always performed the rite of protection, should subsequently recite the mantra.

"One should show the stations of yoga" means that yoga is meditative absorption (*samādhi*), while the "stations" (*sthāna*) are the limbs (*aṅga*); one should show them, which is to say, one should thus armor [them].

"One should not transgress the weapons" means that one should not step over the armor and so forth as previously described. Alternatively, "weapons" refers to the messengers (dūtīs), who are like weapons; one should not transgress them.
Or else, "weapons" refers to the insignia of oneself and others.
A person who observes the commitments should not revile; one must never engage in reviling.
"One should not approach those who are engaged" means that in this tantra or in another tantra, one should not approach anyone who is currently engaged [in practice].
The meaning is that one should enjoy pleasure together with them—that is, one should share a single meal (or a single remnant) with those who hold the pledges (*samayinī*).
Alternatively, "pleasure" (*sukha*) refers to the means; the meaning is that one should employ the means for the attainment of Mahāmudrā. Or, *sukham* may be another reading [for *saham*].
And one who desires the self and desires that goal, having thus become constantly engaged in yoga, should practice day and night during the four periods of the day; this is the meaning.
Regarding the phrase "by means of the conduct of the *samaya*": *samaya* refers to the deities; their conduct is [the conduct of the *samaya*], and it is from that.
Alternatively, *samaya* refers to [rules] such as what is to be observed and what is not to be consumed.

"Then indeed, wandering, he is released from activity"—the word "vai" (indeed) signifies certainty; the meaning is that the wandering yogi is released from activity and becomes liberated as he pleases.
"He is constantly naked at night"—this is indeed the literal truth.
"He should always be black-red" means that he should be wandering at night. "Clothing made from the limb of a living being" means that he is covered with a garment of skin.
"One who desires pleasure and seeks that [pleasure] should move for the sake of pleasure" means one should produce the pleasure of sexual union (surata).

The meaning is that by completely abandoning the sacrificial thread (*yajñopavīta*)—that is, by relinquishing the purification (*śauca*) prescribed by the Vedas and Smṛtis regarding the sacrificial thread—one comes to practice all mundane and supramundane purification through the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of Śrī Heruka.
The five mudrās are the bracelet, the crest-jewel, the necklace, the earrings, and the sacred thread; one should never be separated from these five.

"Free from the rejection of caste or non-caste, and devoid of the binding of topknots and the like": the "face" (*mukha*) of caste and non-caste refers to their investigation; the "rejection" (*ākṣepa*) of that is its avoidance. "Devoid of the binding of topknots and the like" means that the binding of matted hair and so forth should not be performed; by the word "and the like" (*ādi*), other worldly customs are excluded.

[27.4] The passage beginning with "the messengers" (*dūtayaḥ*) and so forth is easy to understand.
