[27.5] Regarding "he is to be honored and indeed purified": he is "to be honored" (*saṃpūjya*) because he abides together with these aforementioned offerings; he is "purified" (*viśuddhas*) because his purpose has been fulfilled through the supreme, unsurpassed worship.
"Nirvāṇa" means "gone forth"; the meaning is that one should worship the Hero immediately after the state of the supreme bliss of great passion (*paramasurata*).
By him who has worshipped himself through outer and secret offerings, the entire world—including all things animate and inanimate—has been worshipped.

"One should worship those who practice with one's brothers" means that the practitioner of yoga (*yogacārī*) should do so together with one who has entered a single maṇḍala or similar state; with him, the union of the moon (*somasaṃgama*) should be performed by means of the bones.

"Arising from pleasure and pain together with brothers and sons" means that, like worldly people, one should not reveal knowledge such as the *mahāmudrā* or the mantra-seals (*mantramudrā*) together with brothers, sons, and so forth.

"One should eat the *caru* [oblation], having always performed the purifications and the conduct of the pledge (*samayācāra*). The meaning is that by eating the *caru*, the conduct of the pledge is accomplished, and consequently, one becomes pure.
"One should not give the mantra to anyone" means exactly as it says.
"The messenger (dūtī) is always liberation" means that during the state of sexual union (*surata*), the external woman is to be protected by the great armor (*mahākavaca*) and other such mantras.
"Even if there is a transgression, one should feed her"—this means that if she is exceptionally well-trained, fortunate, and a woman of noble character, one should prepare her [food] and feed her.

"And one should certainly not show honor [to those] who are established in the delight of inferior birth"—here, "birth" refers to families such as the Brahmins and so forth; however, this should not be accepted [as the primary criterion], for the meaning is that because they are unfit for the supreme yoga, no respect should be shown toward them.

Regarding the passage beginning with "mātā" (mother) and so forth: the meaning is that one should practice with any woman—such as a mother, daughter, and so on—who possesses the characteristics of a messenger (*dūtī*); otherwise, one's asceticism and other virtues will be exhausted.
"One should attract the supreme [deity] together"—thus, in the ritual procedure for attracting the Moon, no alternative option should be made.
Thus, the determination of the substance means the determination of the ultimate reality itself; this is the meaning.
"Vāma" and so forth are exactly according to the facts.
The meaning is that by the rule of conduct "intent upon that once," the mantra-practitioner who eats the sacrificial porridge (caru) at a single location shall quickly attain accomplishment.
The remainder is exactly as it appears in the source text.
By means of the passage beginning with "cow-flesh" and so forth, that which was taught is for the purpose of destroying those beings who harm the followers of the teaching.

The procedure for this is as follows: having constructed a triangular sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) according to the rules prescribed in the *Homopāyikā*, and having kindled it with pungent oils and other substances suitable for a fierce (*krūra*) oblation according to the stated injunctions, one should visualize Khaṇḍarohā entering through the right nostril and emerging via the exhaled breath. With her hands grasping a vajra-hook (*vajrāṅkuśa*) and a knife (*karttarī*), she draws forth the target (*sādhya*)—who has become naked and overwhelmed—and one should contemplate that very goddess cutting him into pieces. Then, with beef and other meats as prescribed...
Thinking, "The flesh of that [victim] to be slain has been obtained," one should offer oblations with the root mantra while possessed by great wrath and the ego-sense, saying, "Kill so-and-so!"
"Citrinām" refers to the capture of either a peacock or a cock.

"Likewise, the food of the heroes is accompanied by the mudrās and mantras": the meaning is that the food which is accompanied by—that is, joined with—an external woman who consists of mantra and mudrā and is well-trained in the mantra-tantras, becomes commendable for the heroes.
"Manifestation" (nirmāṇa) is a synonym for the very mind of awakening (bodhicitta).
The remainder is easy to understand.
His messenger is the goddess;
she is supreme, that is, most excellent.
Diligent and untiring,
accompanied by companions, she does not turn back.
Thus it becomes divine;
the meaning is that it becomes fit for accomplishment (siddhi).
The meaning of "due to the absence of conjunction with passion" is that no experience of conjunction with passion occurs in its natural form.
Yoga is meditative absorption (samādhi), and substance (dravya) is that which is to be consumed; the "division" (vibhāga) refers to the separation between these two.
Alternatively, yoga is a connection (saṃbandha), and substance is that which is connected; the remainder of the sentence is that there is no division between these two.
"Deeply colored by the guru’s instruction" means that one should not destroy the succession of the lineage of gurus.
For that purpose, by approaching the Giver of Wealth (Dhanada) and acting according to the meaning as it has been explained, one becomes equal to Śrī Heruka;
[one regards] the hero as a brother and Śrī Heruka as a father.
The meaning is: "In an instant he perceives lordship; in an instant he sees by means of lordship."
The meaning is that one endowed with characteristics such as a thick tongue and so forth becomes a common or ordinary [vessel] for all accomplishments (*siddhi*).
It is endowed with recollection and possessed of the characteristics of the five nectars.

"Endowed with the words 'messenger' (dūtī) and so forth" means that through the constant practice of yoga, he is joined with the messenger; by the word "and so forth" (ādi), it is meant that the mantra-practitioner abides in the vows regarding what is to be protected and what is to be consumed.
In that regard, there are twenty-four principal stationary ḍākinīs who bestow the fruits of enjoyment and liberation.
The remainder is easy to understand.
By means of the application of the object of focus for the superior meditative concentration (*atiśaya-samādhi*) within the entire self,
"the activity of heat" (*ūṣma-kriyā*) is mentioned as an illustration.
The stages of Heat (ūṣman), Summits (mūrdhan), Patience (kṣānti), and Supreme Mundane Dharmas (agradharma) are to be understood according to their respective meanings.
Alternatively, "the activity of heat" (ūṣmakriyā) refers to one who possesses the power of yoga.
The passage beginning with "they hate" (dviṣanti) and so forth is easy to understand.
With the words beginning with "atha," he extracts the mantra of Sumbha and Niṣumbha.
"Then, having formed a *muraja-bandha*," means that one should draw it in the shape of a drum (*muraja*), consisting of forty-nine squares.
"The third from the square" is said with reference to the fourth square from the center;
among those vowels, the third is the letter *sa*.
For this very reason it has been said: "The practitioner [should practice] the vowels and consonants both in direct and reverse order."
"By the fifth" means from the first square of the vowels.
"By half of half of a hundred" means starting from the letter *ka*.
"By twenty-four" is likewise [to be understood] in the same way.
The "thirty-sixth of the belly" refers to the letter *na*, beginning from the letter *a*.
"By means of the three compartments" is likewise.
"Thirty-two" refers to the letter *sa*, starting from the letter *ka*.
By "the fifth of the chest" is meant the letter *u*.
The twenty-fifth [letter] is from the letter *ka*.
"By twenty-four," it is just as before.
"By the thirty-third" refers to the letter *ka*.
"Fifteen" [is derived] from the vowel *a*.
"By the fifth" means by the fifth vowel.
"The twenty-second" refers to the letter *ka*.
And it is precisely the twenty-seventh because of the letter *a*.
This is the first word of the mantra.
From the letter *a* onwards, there are nineteen letters up to the letter *ga*.
The son of Fire is the letter *ra*.
The letter *i* is the third in the group.
The passage beginning with "yavarge" and so forth is easy to understand.
The letter *na* [is added] as before, for the thirty-sixth.
"Once again" means that one should give those same two syllables once more.
The letter *ha* is "the Self-Existent" (*svayaṃbhū*).
"By the fifth cell" means from the vowel-cell.
"By the bindu" means by the anusvāra.
The second word is the remainder as before; as before, there are nineteen *ga* syllables.
"Starting from *ka* and so forth, up to thirty-seven" means beginning from the letter *ka*.
"By the third" means by the third vowel.
"Thirty-three" is as before; [the letter] *ha*.
The second letter from the chest is the form "ā".
The twentieth [letter], beginning from *ka*, is indeed *na*.

Due to the continued application of the rule "after *ra* and *ṣ*, and after a homogeneous vowel following a reduplicated syllable, *na* becomes *ṇa* within the same word," the *na* following the word *gṛha-* in forms such as *aṭ-kuṣṭhāṇ-ṇaḥ* undergoes the change to *ṇa*.
Starting from the letter *ka*, the twenty-first is the letter *pa*.
Likewise, there are twenty-six.
"The repetition twice" is as explained previously.
In reverse order, the first syllable of the *koṣṭha* is the letter *ha*.
The fourth is the vowel *ī*; at its end is the vowel *u*.
The remainder is as before.
Now he states the extraction of the fourth line.
"From the second cell of the [first] row," and so forth, means starting from the first cell of the vowels.
"Thirty-sixth" refers to the letter beginning with *a*.
And it is indeed the twenty-sixth, starting from the letter *ka*.
"Trāyastriṃśa" is likewise [to be understood] in the same way.
"Thirteenth" means the thirteenth vowel.
"The tenth from the square" means the letter *bha*, counting backwards starting from the letter *ha*.
The nineteenth from the square, beginning with the letter *a*.
There are twenty-nine [syllables] beginning with the letter *ka*.
"Second from the square" means from the square of the vowels.
"By the bindu" means conjoined with the anusvāra at the top.
The letter *va* is [the essence of] "pārthiva" (the earthly).
The eighth is the letter ja.
"One should always pierce with fire"—that is, one should pierce with the syllable *repha* (the letter *r*).
The remainder is easy to understand.
"In the Root Tantra" means in the *Paramādya-tantra*.
"Endowed with the four wrathful ones" refers to the four words of the mantra, which denote the four wrathful kings whose names have not yet been specified.
"Endowed with the eight forms" means that this mantra consists of the eight forms beginning with earth (kṣiti).
By this mantra, "He dies as soon as this is obtained," one who has entered the womb is pacified.
One should offer the *mahāmāṃsa* as before; thus it becomes as it was described.
*Tāmracūḍa* means a cock.
Regarding the phrase "the hero wearing a garland of skulls, adorned with the half-moon," that which was not previously mentioned concerning the Blessed One is here completed.

As for the instruction "one should show the five *cchommakas*," here the word *cchommaka* is used figuratively to refer to the five deities beginning with Vajravārāhī; the meaning is that one should show and meditate upon the five deities within the five skulls adorned with the crown of matted hair.

"The practitioner with the left hand" means that whatever food, drink, or other edibles there may be, all of that should be given by the practitioner with his left hand when being offered to those who share his commitments (samasayin). This is the meaning.
The remainder is easy to understand.
With the words beginning "Vajrasattva," he demonstrates the hand-offering (*hastapūjā*).
"Vajrasattva resides on the thumb-tarjanī"—this should be connected to all [the fingers].
Vairocana is on the index finger of the creeper-gesture.
For the Guru, on the middle finger, is Padmanartaka; thus [he is called] Padmanarteśvara.
On the ring finger of the *dhārā* [hand] is "Vīra," which is Śrī Heruka.
*Tanu* refers to the little finger; *avyaya* is an adjective qualifying that very [finger]; therein resides Ākāśagarbha, who is Vajrasūrya.
"By means of the two fingernails" refers to Hayagrīva, who resides within the nails of all the fingers.
"The cause of the arising of the left" means that the left hand is their cause or support.

Regarding "on the palm of the hand": having visualized a five-petaled lotus on the palm of the hand, one should meditate that upon the filaments of the lotus are the female messengers: Vajravārāhī in front, Yāminī to her left, Mohanī behind her, Saṃcālanī to her right, and Trāsanī and Caṇḍikā, eager for union, on the other side; thus they are of the same intention as oneself.

Regarding the phrase "one should make a firm determination on the back [of the hand]," although deities such as Vajrasattva and others, as well as Vajravārāhī and others, have been specified by means of the seed-mantra on the palm, the meaning is that one should meditate with certainty upon them on the back of the hand as if they were reflections seen within a mirror.
For this very reason, he will later state: "The wise one should dismiss them from the back."

Regarding the statement "five secret signs (cchommaka) are to be shown by the practitioner," because of the repetition of the word "five," in this context of the hand-worship (hastapūjā), the five secret signs refer to the five [substances] beginning with feces and urine.
By the mention of Locanā and the others, the four [consorts] beginning with Ḍākinī are intended.
"Empty" refers to the element of space.
"In the middle" refers to that very same thing.
The remainder is easy to understand.

"One should signal the hero with signs" means that by means of hand-gestures (*hastapūjā*) and substances such as those contained within the great conch, one should signal—that is, worship—the hero, Śrī Heruka.
Thereafter, one should take the sacrificial pap (*caru*), which is to say, one should consume it.
When this is done, in the assembly of all heroes, there occurs the *Ḍākinījālasaṃvara*.
By means of the previously mentioned procedure, the practitioner performs the summoning of the sacrificial victim (*paśu*).
He says, "domestic animals.
This refers to those of the five-nailed species, such as the dog, the cat, the hare, and so forth;
and humans and others are included according to their actual nature.

Regarding the phrase "among the castes": among the four castes beginning with the Kṣatriya, he is described as a "beast" (*paśu*); thus, a "hero-beast" (*vīrapaśu*) is one by whom many heroes have been slain, or one who has been seen through the transformation into Heruka.
Regarding animals, those born from the animal womb: "animal" in the sense of a beast refers to a serpent, and gems are also considered animals.
This sacrificial animal also becomes a means for the happiness of the gods.

Specific types of birds, beginning with crows and ending with the kādamba, are to be employed in the rites of *homa* and *bali*. *Homa* here refers specifically to the internal *homa* (*antarhoma*). Now, he explains the accomplishment of the Great Preta, beginning with the words "black" (*kṛṣṇa*) and so forth.

First, having performed the preliminary service (*pūrvasevā*) of either the *sumbhanisumbha* mantra or the root mantra, and having obtained the signs and so forth, the practitioner should seek out a corpse that is unbroken and undecayed in a cremation ground. At midnight during the dark fortnight, he should perform a fire offering (*homa*) at the dead of night using black dog’s milk, black beans (*māṣa*), and turbid rice.

"Without hesitation in the mouth of the corpse" means that even though the practitioner who has realized yoga has performed protective rites such as the triple enclosure, the cage, and the great armor, he should not give rise to fear;
or rather, the sense is that upon seeing a great preta, variously terrifying and deformed, one should not feel fear.
The remainder is easy to understand; there is no doubt that it will be as described.
Regarding the "cow-pen lotus" (*goṣṭhotpalikā*), it is a specific type of ash.
As for the "dry skull," having taken a dry, unbroken human head, one should fashion it into a great conch (*mahāśaṅkha*).
Or a tortoise skull.
With the words "four-armed" and so forth, he demonstrates the mahāmudrā of the Blessed One, Śrī Heruka.
All of this is explained in detail in the *Sādhanopāyikā*.
"Assuming his color and bearing his weapon" means she whose nature is to assume the color and weapon of that Blessed One; the meaning is that she is black in color and bears the vajra as her weapon.
Although "weapon" (*āyudha*) is a general term, because it is his primary emblem, the *vajra* alone is mentioned.
For even though he bears many emblems, the Blessed One is designated as "Vajradhara" (the Vajra-Holder).
"Adorned with the body of mudrās" means by means of the five mudrās.
"With a great preta as his seat" means he has trampled upon the lord of spirits.
"Then one should meditate on the mantra"—the meaning is that one should not recite the mantra without the focal point of the great yoga.
The remainder is exactly as it appears in the text.

Regarding the statement "it should be performed even when not present, using the five foods": the intended meaning is that when the commitment of the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta-samaya*) is absent, one should then conceptually transform whatever food is available into the nature of the five nectars.
"At night," and so forth, is easy to understand.
The seats, mudrās, and deities of the heroes [are as follows].

"Susamāhita" (well-concentrated) should be understood as the employment of song, instrumental music, and so forth, in a non-ordinary manner. "Afterwards, one should practice the heroism of the heroes" means that first, having performed the worship of the deity as previously described to the utmost degree, one should afterwards practice the heroism of the heroes, such as the Mahāmudrā and other [mudrās].
Alternatively, with the words "or else" and so forth, one should worship the triple wheel, which consists of three wheels.
*Kalāra* is that which is both a part (*kalā*) and a spoke (*āra*); in that [wheel], there is a hero (*vīra*). The singular number is used with reference to their common genus.
The plural form "in the Puṣkaras" is used because they occupy the position of a preceptor.

"One should place the *avadhūta* position between the eyebrows, likewise"—the meaning is that one should display that which is called *avadhūta*, the "uneven eye," as the accomplished position or station produced by the rays of the *vajramālā* on the forehead, [placing it] between the eyebrows on the forehead.
With the words beginning "Vīrocchuṣma," he explains the fire-offering (*homā*) for all ritual actions.
For the sake of the hero Śrī Heruka, when passion has become withered and one is in a state of wrath, one should offer oblations—that is, perform a fire sacrifice—with flesh.
Alternatively, the intended meaning is that first, one should satisfy oneself with whatever flesh is available while maintaining a sense of wrathful ego.
Thereafter, in accordance with the specific ritual action, one should quickly and swiftly offer five oblations of beef mixed with its blood.
"With effort" means that one should then offer nine oblations with the identification of oneself as the deity.

When the sacrificial fire is ablaze like an ocean of garlands of flames—that is, when the fire-tongues have become very abundant—fuel such as sacrificial wood and the like should be offered according to the requirements of the specific rite.

Having thus made the oblation into the mouth of the fire deity, he explains the procedure for the oblation to one's chosen deity (iṣṭadevatā) who is endowed with the three wheels, beginning with the words "Then," and so forth.

One should see the wheel facing in all directions; thus, one should meditate upon the three-tiered gabled palace within the center of the sacrificial pit, complete with its enclosure wall, endowed with its own colors, arms, and seals, according to the rules.
To explain this in part, he says "four-faced" and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "one should place Khaṇḍarohā on the outside": having likewise stationed Khaṇḍarohā on the petal at the back, one should, in accordance with the ritual action, emanate another Khaṇḍarohā from one's own body and place her on the outside; the meaning is that this is for the sake of accomplishing all ritual activities (*sarvakarmaprasādhana*).
For this very reason it was said: "One should show those who are situated within one's own bodies as being in the center of the wheel."

"One should produce the radiance of the wheel for him, according to the sequence"—this means that one should construct this sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) in the shape of three wheels, following the sequence of the rites for pacification (*śānti*) and so forth without transgression.
"The Tantra named *Vidyārṇava*": the meaning is that what was explained there, O Hero, in brief, has been made clear here.
Alternatively, the intention is that it was explained in the *Vidyārṇava*, while here the procedure is given in summary, whereas there it was extensive.
The remainder is easy to understand.
Now, with the words "from this" (*ataḥ*) and so forth, he explains the procedure for the recitation of mantras and meditation according to the specific ritual action (*karman*).

Regarding the phrase "mantras joined together with one another": as in the case of a cruel rite, the mantra-syllables—joined to one another like a well-twisted rope, emerging simultaneously from both ends, and having the form of a rotating water-wheel (ghaṭīyantra)—are to be visualized.
"Vīrāḥ" refers to the syllables of the mantra.

Regarding the phrase "pierced by entry": in the rite of pacification (*śānti*), the mantra-syllables enter within from one's own mouth; they take the form of a chain or a cord, are emitted through the path of the *vajra*, and then enter again through the path of the lotus into the womb of the deity. From the mouth of the deity, they return to one's own mouth—this is the sequence.
In the rite of cruelty (*krūra*), however, the distinction is that [the syllables proceed] from one's own mouth through the sequence of the deity's mouth.
In pacification, they are relaxed and not harsh.
Then, the seed-syllable garland—meaning the garland of phonemes—is devoured, being mutually entwined with one another.

"Established within the syllable *hūṃ*" means that for a cruel rite, one should suppress [the mantra] with the syllable *hūṃ* at the beginning, middle, and end. For this very reason it was said: "Through suppression, however, the object of accomplishment (*sādhya*) shall become [subdued]; he does not go to a single state"—this is easy to understand. "Encased" (*saṃpuṭa*) means by way of being encased; according to the sequence taught in the *Mantravyākaraṇa* and other texts, it is "encased" by having the syllable *oṃ* at the beginning and the syllable *oṃ* at the end. Thus, it is "by way of being encased."
Oṃ devadatta svāhā oṃ.

"One should pierce with the vajra by means of the vajra-chain binding" means that because the *saṃpuṭa* [mantra] is effective for all ritual actions (*sarvakarmika*), when it is associated with a rite of forceful action (*krūrakarman*), one should then pierce with the vajra, which is the syllable *hūṃ*.
"One should whirl the brush" means that one should whirl the brush continuously, just as it is seen to be done continuously.

"One should attract with the hook" means that when an attraction is intended, one should attract by means of Khaṇḍarohā, who holds a hook in her hand, having interwoven the mantra according to the method of the sprout and the leaf.

Regarding "likewise, the pestle for agitation": when the agitation of an army or similar force is intended, then one should agitate the entire army and so forth by means of Khaṇḍarohā, who holds a pestle.

"Grasping is said to be the vajra" means that during grasping—that is, consuming—one should consume [the victim] by means of the fierce rite, thinking, "Having seized it with the vajra, one shall eat it."
"Vedhana" refers to shaking; it was performed by Khaṇḍarohā, who held an arrow in her hand.

And regarding the deception of timely death: at the time of death, one should perform the conquest of death; [the goddess] with a skull-topped staff held in her hand should be visualized on the left side of the body, like the edge of a sword.
Khaṇḍarohā excels by means of all these various types of weapons.

"One should offer the *argha* with a skull-cup; the application of the weapon (*astra*) to the mouth" means that, having offered the *argha* into the mouth of Khaṇḍarohā which is filled with the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*), one should perform the application of the weapon; the meaning is that one should display it like a garland of mantra-syllables.
"In the immobilization of the mudrās, the action is eating" means that in the immobilization of the supreme mudrās, one should begin the ritual action as if eating, like consuming food.

"The mantra-practitioner should likewise join [the offerings] with the hearts of the ḍākinīs"—that is to say, the ritual should be performed in that manner using either the hearts or the mantras of the ḍākinīs.

"Having understood the procedure for the worship of the heroes, one should perform the rite with diligence"—having performed the worship of the heroes according to the procedure stated here, one should subsequently commence the ritual action.

"Having divided [them] at will, the mantra-practitioner should employ them in reverse"—this means that having divided and separated them according to the nature of the rite, the mantra-practitioner should apply the rites in their opposite form.
To indicate this very point, he says "nigraha," etc.

"Divided among the divisions of the principles (*tattva*) and joined to the paths of the channels (*nādīmārga*)," means: the divisions are the various manifestations of activity (*karmaprasara*) of the principles; the mantras have been divided—that is, separated—among them, and they are "joined," that is, applied, to the paths of the channels, which are the paths of the vajra and lotus; they are to be shown—this is the connection. [36.2]

"One should accomplish the goal of yoga; by this, one should quickly subdue those consisting of gods, asuras, and humans"—here, "the goal of yoga" means for the sake of attaining the accomplishment of Mahāmudrā. That which has been excellently taught as the "accomplishment" (prasādhana) is that by means of this practice (*sādhana*), one should quickly—that is, swiftly—subdue even gods, asuras, and humans in the form of both restraint and grace.
The intended meaning is: "How much more so others?
Now, with the words beginning with "atha," he demonstrates the ritual applications (*prayoga*) such as subjugation (*vaśya*).

The term *vigraha* means the body; those people, such as women and others, who are possessed by that [body]—the means for their accomplishment, such as subjugation (*vaśīkaraṇa*) and so forth, he shall now explain with the words beginning "therefore" (*ataḥ*). Thus, with these words and others, he describes the procedure for the recitation of mantras and meditation according to the specific ritual action (*karman*).

Regarding the phrase "mantras joined with one another": as in the case of a cruel rite, the syllables of the mantra should be visualized as being joined to one another like a well-twisted rope, emerging simultaneously from both ends, having the form of a rotating water-wheel (*ghaṭīyantra*).
"Vīrāḥ" refers to the syllables of the mantra.

"But they are split by entry" means that in the rite of pacification (*śānti*), the mantra-syllables enter within from one's own mouth, taking the form of a chain or a cord; they are emitted through the path of the *vajra*, and then again enter the womb of the deity through the path of the *padma*. The sequence is: from the mouth of the deity back to one's own mouth.
However, in the rite of cruelty (*krūra*), the distinction is that [the syllables proceed] from one's own mouth through the sequence of the deity's mouth.
In pacification, they are relaxed and not harsh.
Then, the seed-syllable garland—that is, the garland of syllables—is swallowed, being mutually entwined with one another.
"Established within the *hūṃ* syllable" means that for a cruel rite, one should suppress [the mantra] with the *hūṃ* syllable at the beginning, middle, and end;
therefore it is said: "Through suppression, however, the target becomes subdued and does not go to another state"—this is easy to understand.

"The *saṃpuṭa*" means by way of being encapsulated (*saṃpuṭībhāvena*), according to the sequence taught in the *Mantravyākaraṇa* and other texts, as an encapsulation from the *oṃ* syllable at the beginning to the *oṃ* syllable at the end. By "being encapsulated," it is meant that it is enclosed.
Oṃ devadatta svāhā oṃ.

"One should pierce with the vajra by means of the vajra-chain binding" means that because the *saṃpuṭa* [mantra] performs all ritual actions (*sarvakarmika*), when it is associated with a fierce rite (*krūrakarman*), one should then pierce with the vajra, that is, with the syllable *hūṃ*.
"One should whirl the whisk (picchaka) likewise" means that one should whirl the whisk continuously, just as it is seen to be done continuously.

"One should attract with the hook (aṅkuśa)" means that when an attraction is desired, one should attract by means of Khaṇḍarohā, who holds a hand grasping a hook, having interwoven the mantra according to the method of the sprout and the leaf.

Regarding "likewise the pestle for agitation": when the agitation of an army or similar force is intended, then one should agitate the entire army and so forth by means of Khaṇḍarohā holding a pestle.

"In swallowing, it is said to be the vajra" means that in swallowing—that is, in eating—one should eat [the victim] by means of the fierce rite, thinking, "I shall eat such-and-such, having seized them with the vajra."
"Vedhana" means shaking; it was performed by Khaṇḍarohā, who held an arrow in her hand.

And also for the deception of timely death: at the time of death, one should perform the conquest of death; [visualizing her] with a skull-topped staff held in her hand upon her left shoulder, like the edge of a sword.
Khaṇḍarohā excels by means of all these various types of weapons.

"One should offer the *argha* with a skull-cup; the application of the *astra* [mantra] to the mouth" means that, having offered the *argha* into the mouth of Khaṇḍarohā with one filled with the five nectars (*pañcāmṛta*), one should perform the application of the *astra*, which is to say, one should display it like a garland of mantra syllables.
Regarding "the act of eating in the immobilization of the mudrās," one should begin the ritual action as if eating, just as in the immobilization of the supreme mudrās.

"The mantra practitioner should join [the practice] with the hearts of the ḍākinīs, and likewise with these"—this means that the ritual procedure should be performed in that manner by means of the heart-mantras of the ḍākinīs.

"Having understood the ritual for the worship of the heroes, one should perform the rite with diligence"—the connection here is that, having performed the worship of the heroes according to the procedure stated in this context, one should proceed as follows.
"Mantras entwined with one another" means that the root-mantras of both are unified;
"and the ḍākinīs joined together in one place" clarifies that very same meaning.
In this regard, the sequence is as follows:

Having vomited up what was eaten and having thoroughly washed it, one should mix it with the five bodily impurities and undissolved camphor; then, reciting both root mantras at the four junctions of the day for seven days, one should subsequently employ it in food and drink. As it has been stated, there is no doubt that it will come to pass.
"Of Kapilā" means a cow of tawny color.
The remainder is easy to understand.
The passage beginning with "abhyaṅga" and so forth, as well as that beginning with "bhakṣayitvā" and so forth, is likewise clearly explained.

If one performs a fire offering (homa) with beef and its blood in either the *vaśya* hearth or the all-purpose (*sarvakarmika*) hearth while reciting the name of someone, the deities—those heroes and others—will come under control;
they will certainly bring them under subjection, provided that it is done as prescribed. Otherwise, it will not happen.
"In front of him" means in front of Śrī Heruka;
by the word "or" (vā), it means [in] the mouth.
The remainder is easy to understand.
The differentiation of limbs refers to the color, face, arms, weapons, and so forth.
"And he is not defiled, O Lord of Heroes" means that the Blessed One does not perceive one who transgresses the rules of conventional conduct (*samayācāra*).
"One should not recite," and so forth, is exactly as it states.
And "he finds the tradition" means that he experiences whatever happiness exists in the three worlds.
"With sections" means with groups.
"One should place the fourfold laughter" means that there is a fourfold [laughter] belonging to the root mantra of Vīra.
kili 2 sili 2 cili 2 dhili 2 / this is the root mantra of the ḍākinī: hā hā he he ho ho hūṃ hūṃ.
With the words beginning "now" (*adhunā*), he describes the general method for bringing kings and others under one's control.

Regarding the phrase "of this [offering] consisting of flesh and so forth, together with fish and meat": "flesh and so forth" is stated generally to indicate the sacrificial materials; "of this" refers to the oblation (*homa*). And that oblation is of two kinds: external oblation (*bāhyahoma*) and bodily oblation (*kāyahoma*); for this very reason it is said, "together with fish and meat."
Even in every state, even in a state of being angry or pleased.
Vīreśa is Śrī Heruka;
the connection is that he bestows vast accomplishment upon the practitioner.
"Devoted to the fire-oblation at night"—thus, the bodily oblation must certainly be performed during the night.
The passage beginning with "by seven" and so forth is easy to understand.
Now, by the passage beginning with "then action," it is shown that the yogin who has attained perfection possesses the accomplishment of all activities.
The statement "twelve" is made with reference to the unification of subjugation (*vaśya*) and attraction (*ākarṣaṇa*), and the unification of killing (*māraṇa*) and driving away (*uccāṭana*).
By the passage beginning with "in all the higher [realms]," the locations of the twenty-four *ḍākinīs* are revealed.
The Vajra-maṇḍala is the Śrī Heruka maṇḍala;
therein, the female leaders are the primary figures.
The wilderness is a desert region.
Āraṇa is Rāmeśvara.

Pullīramalaya has not been specifically mentioned; it is to be understood as such because it is the foremost of all *pīṭhas*, or because of the oral instruction (*upadeśa*). All [the sites] beginning with Pullīramalaya are to be taken in reverse order, encompassing all the cardinal and intermediate directions.
The six *yoginīs* range from Vajravārāhī to Caṇḍikā.
The Mothers are Kākāsyā and the others.
"Lāmās" refers to the fierce yoginīs belonging to the Lāmā class.
The four ḍākinīs who are the leaders of the families.
Mahākāla, Mahābhairava.
The instrumental case in "with the ḍākinīs" (ḍākinībhiḥ) is used in the sense of accompaniment.
Accompanied by what kind? By the Rūpiṇīs.
It should be understood that "together with the Rūpiṇīs" refers to other distinct [ḍākinīs] such as Rūpiṇī, Cumbikā, Āsavālikā, and so forth.
Pañcāla is a distinct sacred site of the Siddhas, separate from the pīṭhas and upapīṭhas.
These and others have been mentioned as representative examples;
in detail, however, twenty-one thousand *siddhayoginīs* wander everywhere in various forms.
Furthermore, the goddesses who preside over the three wheels (*tricakravartinī*), such as Pracaṇḍā and the rest, are to be associated with locations beginning with Pullīramalaya in reverse order.
The other remaining deities are also the yoginīs of Śrī Heruka;
"Mahāmanthāna" refers to those who are suitable for the churning of Śrī Heruka.
The genitive case in "tāsām" is used in the sense of selection (nirdhāraṇa).
"The leaders of the mandala" refers to the twenty-four ḍākinīs who preside over the three wheels; the connection is that [the body] is pervaded by these together with them.

Regarding the term *sacarācaram*: it refers to the moving and non-moving [beings] upon the various earths, by means of an external consort (*bāhyāṅganā*) who is perfect, possesses a non-natural form, and is fit for the act of churning and being churned. Furthermore, of what nature is she? She is "without another accumulation" (*aparacayā*);
that is, no other accumulation or heap (*caya-rāśi*) exists [of her].
That which has an accumulation on the other side is "aparacayā.
Alternatively, here the nominative case should be understood as the instrumental;
the connection is that he remains naked with her at all times, even at night.
The rest is according to the literal meaning.
*Kusumodaka* (flower-water) arises together with a woman who has her menses.
"This mantra" refers either to the root mantra or the seven-syllable mantra.

Mahākālī by truth, Vajravārāhī by truth, she who is the practitioner of celibacy.

Laughter itself is the mudrā; for by means of laughter characterized primarily by playfulness, which brings satisfaction, there is sealing (mudraṇa) [of the mind].

"One should perform [the rite] with this" means with this [verse].

the connection is that one should perform all the pleasures of great *mahāsura* at night or during the day.
By means of the phrase "the ritual of form" (*rūpakarma*) and so forth, the deities whose accomplishments have been realized through the practitioner's vision perform unprecedented acts of form.

By the words "one should perform" and so forth, he demonstrates that this [practice] is to be kept secret through its extraordinary nature as a form of worship.
With the words beginning with "kusuma," he states the cause for the practitioner's possession of all powers:

when one has consecrated a handful of flowers with the mantra and casts them into the sky, if not even a single flower falls to the ground, then at that time one is capable of accomplishing everything; such is the detailed explanation.
"It is not seen by gods or humans" means that it does not exist for any god or human.
By means of the seven-syllable mantra beginning with "vṛkṣa," he demonstrates the preliminary service (*pūrvasevā*) and various types of ritual procedures (*vidhi*).
The meaning is that it increases the lifespan of one who has been struck by untimely death or is lost, removes death, and restores the vital essence of one whose strength has perished.
With the words beginning with "khaḍga," he shows the procedure for sharpening.
By the words beginning with "dhyāta" (meditated upon), he demonstrates the pacification of disease.

Whether the seven-syllable mantra is meditated upon, or recited a hundred times, or directly placed within the center of the sun—having stationed there the patient who is afflicted by disease, one should then rotate it a thousand times. One should meditate on his body as being stainless like pure crystal; thus it becomes as described.

Furthermore, by perceiving what is similar, one should touch upon the consciousness within that heart—which is the size of a thumb, as pure as crystal, and of a blazing, radiant form—and thus one becomes well-established.
With the words beginning "In the autumn season," he describes the removal of poison;
that is easy to understand.
Regarding "the fivefold form": when a circle of the moon is made with five squares, a nine-square grid is produced;
this is the arrangement of the moon therein.

Having placed this upon the head of one who has been seized by the poison of a stationary or moving creature, one should meditate on their entire body becoming free of poison through streams of nectar; thus, the person becomes restored to health.
In this manner, one should also dispel fevers and other ailments;
furthermore, the instruction is that the practitioner himself should consume food, edibles, and so forth in this same way.
The passage beginning with "māṃsa" (flesh) and so forth is easy to understand.

Having seen this very yantra on the palm of the hand, one should hold it to the head; the previously mentioned result for the person to be acted upon (*sādhya*) occurs. [43] "Pure milk" (*śaucakṣīra*) means cow's milk. [44] "Horse-killer" (*aśvamāra*) means *karavīra*.
"Having formed the *yonimudrā*" means having united with an external woman.

Regarding the instruction "one should smear with beeswax," the construction should be understood as follows: having fashioned an image out of beeswax, one should smear it with the powder of red sandalwood and the three pungent spices (trikaṭuka). [45]

"One should rub the five *ha*-syllables on the hand"—this means that one should smear the dust from the feet of [the enemy], along with poison, blood, and black mustard seeds, onto the palms of both hands; then, having written the five *ha*-syllables upon them with yellow orpiment, chalk, or the like, using a crow-feather pen, and having visualized them through meditation in that very same way, one should offer oblations by rubbing both hands together over charcoal of *khadira* wood or funeral pyre embers while drawing blood from the mouth; thus the enemy dies.
The same applies to a skull as well.

For this very reason, it is said: "situated within the wheel," and so forth.
Regarding "Mahācakra": the Blessed One is so called because he possesses a great *cakra*, which is a collection; or because he possesses three great *cakras*.

Now, with the words beginning "atha," he explains what was deficient in the previously stated ritual procedure for the animal sacrifice (*paśusādhana*).

"Spitting," and so forth, as well as using a tooth-stick for one's own body, is likewise [prohibited].

By the words beginning with "jāgrat" (while awake), the meaning is that the practitioner of mantra (mantrī) should recite the mantra at all times—whether standing, sitting, eating while accompanied by food remnants, or even engaging in sexual intercourse and so forth;
there is no restriction regarding the time.
It is shown that by performing one hundred oblations daily for one month upon sacrificial fuel such as *arka* wood according to the rite for nourishment (*puṣṭividhi*), all poverty is destroyed.
The passage beginning with "mahāmāṃsa" and so forth is easy to understand.

The intended meaning is that when the mantra-practitioner, having produced the visualization, performs the fire-offering (*homayet*) while remaining in meditative absorption for two watches (*prahara*), he becomes equal to all deities, as it is said: "Everything arises as the deity."

One should offer jackal meat with liquor as an oblation (*homa*). Regarding the phrase "the jackal is restricted for the performance of the *bali*-rite, the recitation (*japa*), and the mantras," it should be connected to this very context.

The intended meaning is that when the *bali*-rite, the recitation, and the mantras have been performed, one should, because of that restriction, consume whatever jackal meat is obtained during the night.
The passage beginning with "of the *śrīphala* fruits" and so forth is to be understood as before, according to the procedure for nourishment (*puṣṭi*).
The passage beginning with "gomāṃsa" (beef) and so forth is easy to understand.

The meaning is as follows: even one who lacks the practice of vows and external purity may attain accomplishment from what has been prescribed; that is to say, although he may not be a practitioner of vows nor possess external cleanliness, nevertheless, by practicing according to this method, the yogi attains accomplishment from the instruction of the deity.
One's lifespan becomes superior and immeasurable.
